say '['format(9.6, 2, 0)']'

[9]
93.942
[10]
[bif.format.after]

after is the count of decimal places. When it is given, the number is rounded to that many places, the magnitude going up when the first dropped digit is 5 or more, or is extended with zeros to that many; and a point separates them from the integer part, unless after is 0, when there is no point. This rounding follows the rounding to NUMERIC DIGITS, and it is not limited by it, so after can ask for more places than NUMERIC DIGITS. When after is omitted, the places are those the number has. A negative number whose value rounds to zero loses its -. This book does not specify the result when the rounding to after carries the first digit to a power of ten above 999999999.

say format(123.456, , 2) format(123.456, , 5) format(123.456, , 0),
    format(-1.235, , 2) format(9.99, , 1) format(0.5, , 0)
say format(-0.4, , 0) format(-0.04, , 1) format(-0.05, , 1) format(-0, , 2)
numeric digits 3
say format(1.2345, , 6) format(12345678, , 1) format(0.12345, , 4)

123.46 123.45600 123 -1.24 10.0 1
0 0.0 -0.1 0.00
1.230000 1.2E+7 0.1230
[bif.format.trigger]

expp and expt control the notation. The trigger T of the writing rule is expt when it is given and NUMERIC DIGITS otherwise. The two counts of that rule are taken at different steps. S, the count of decimal places, is that of the number rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS, so it does not depend on after. W, the count of digits before the point, is that of the number after the rounding to after as well, so a rounding that carries into a new integer digit can make the number scientific. Which of the two tests applies is decided by the number rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS, before after is applied: a number below 1 that after then rounds up to 1 is still tested with S, and a number of 1 or more with W. An expp of 0 overrides the trigger: the result is then always in plain notation, whatever its size. With expp omitted or above 0, the number is written in scientific notation exactly when the writing rule says so for T. A T of 0 therefore makes every number scientific, zero included, unless expp is 0.

say format('12345.5', , , , 5) format('12345.5', , , , 4),
    format('0.00001234', , , , 4) format('0.00001234', , , , 3)
say format('1e30', , , 0) format('1e5', , , , 5) format('1e5', , , , 6)
say format('1e5', , , 0, 5) format('1e5', , , 3, 5) format('0.5', , , , 0)
say format('99999.5', , 0, , 5) format('99999.4', , 0, , 5),
    format('9999.96', , 1, , 4) format('99999.5', , 0, 0, 5)
say format('0.000000123', , 8, , 4) format('0.00000012', , 9, , 4)
numeric digits 3
say format('1e5') format('1e5', , , , 6) format('1.2345', , , 1, 1)
say '['format('0.999', , 0, 2, 1)']' '['format('0.999', , 0, 2, 3)']',
    '['format('1.4', , 0, 2, 1)']'

12345.5 1.23455E+4 0.00001234 1.234E-5
1000000000000000000000000000000 1E+5 100000
100000 1E+005 5E-1
1E+5 99999 1.0E+4 100000
1.23000000E-7 0.000000120
1E+5 100000 1.23
[1    ] [1] [1]
[bif.format.sci]

In scientific notation, after is the count of digits after the point in the part before the E: the digits are rounded to it or extended with zeros, as in the plain case, and with 0 there is no point. A rounding that carries into a new leading digit raises the exponent, so the part before the E keeps the form the notation gives. before is the width of the part before the point. NUMERIC FORM decides the exponent as the notation rule says.

say format('1e30', , 3) format('9.96e10', , 1) format('9.96e10', , 0),
    format('-1.2345e10', , 2)
say '['format('1.2345e10', 5, 1)']' '['format('-1.2345e-20', 3, 2)']'
numeric form engineering
say format('1.2345e10', , 1) format('1e11', 4, 1) format('9.96e10', , 1)

1.000E+30 1.0E+11 1E+11 -1.23E+10
[    1.2E+10] [ -1.23E-20]
12.3E+9  100.0E+9 99.6E+9
[bif.format.expp]

In scientific notation, expp is the width of the exponent: its digits are padded on the left with zeros to expp places, and when it needs more places, the call raises SYNTAX 93.941. The sign + or - is always written. When expp is omitted the exponent has as many digits as it needs. No such error comes from a number written in plain notation, whatever its size.

say format('1e15', , , 2) format('1e-25', , , 3) format('1e150', , , 3),
    format('1e15', , , 2, 16) format('5', , , 3, 6)
signal on syntax name a
say format('1e150', , , 2)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say format('1e-25', , , 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say format('1e999999999', , , 3)
c: say condition('o')~code
say format('1e999999999', , , 9)

1E+15 1E-025 1E+150 1000000000000000 5
93.941
93.941
93.941
1E+999999999
[bif.format.exponent-zero]

A number that is to be in scientific notation but whose exponent would be 0 is written without an exponent. That number is zero, or a result, after the rounding to after, whose magnitude is at least 1 and below 10 (below 1000 under NUMERIC FORM ENGINEERING). When expp is above 0, the result then ends with expp + 2 blanks, the room the exponent would have taken; when expp is omitted nothing follows. An expp of 0 never writes the exponent, and adds no blanks.

say '['format('1.2345', , 2, , 0)']' '['format('1.2345', , 2, 2, 0)']',
    '['format('1.2345', 5, 2, 3, 0)']'
say '['format(0, , , 1, 0)']' '['format(0, 2, 1, 0, 0)']' '['format(50, , , 2, 1)']'
say '['format('-5', , , 1, 0)']' '['format('9.996', , 2, 1, 0)']'
numeric form engineering
say '['format(123, , , 2, 2)']' '['format(123, , , , 2)']' '['format(1234, , , 2, 3)']'
say '['format('-999.4', , , 1, 2)']' '['format('999.6', , 0, 1, 2)']'

[1.23] [1.23    ] [    1.23     ]
[0   ] [ 0.0] [5.0E+01]
[-5   ] [1.00E+1]
[123    ] [123] [1.234E+03]
[-999.4   ] [1E+3]

Note. The ANSI draft (9.4.2) differs from ooRexx, which this book follows, in three ways. It checks number before a count that is not a whole number, where ooRexx raises SYNTAX 40.12 for the count first (for a negative count both check number first), and it raises SYNTAX 40.13 for a negative count and SYNTAX 40.38 for a result that does not fit, in the exponent or in the integer part. It decides the notation before it rounds to after, so there a carry out of the integer part does not make the number scientific: format('99999.5', , 0, , 5) is 100000. And it tests the zeros after the point against a fixed limit, as the note on the writing rule says.

Deviations

[bif.format.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of FORMAT is the same object as another string of equal value: as number itself, when the call leaves it unchanged, or as an equal string produced some other way. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it answers the argument itself in a case where interrexx may answer an equal new string.

s = '12' || '5'
say (format(s) == s) (format('125') == '125') (format(s, 5) == '  125')

1 1 1

FUZZ

FUZZ()

ANSI: 9.5.7; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > FUZZ

FUZZ answers the setting of NUMERIC FUZZ in force where it is called: the count of low-order digits that a numeric comparison ignores.

Arguments

[bif.fuzz.args]

FUZZ takes no arguments. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: none is required and none is the most, so a call with an argument raises SYNTAX 40.4, whatever its value, while a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments. FUZZ does not run as a String method: sending the message FUZZ to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

say fuzz() fuzz( ) fuzz(,)
signal on syntax name a
say fuzz(1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say fuzz('')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say fuzz(, 0)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say 0~fuzz
d: say condition('o')~code

0 0 0
40.4
40.4
40.4
97.1

The result

[bif.fuzz.result]

FUZZ answers the setting as a whole number written without a sign, a point, an exponent or leading zeros. At the start of a program the setting is the default of the package, and the NUMERIC FUZZ instruction changes it, to the value of its expression as a whole number. A setting is a count of digits, so it must stay below the setting of NUMERIC DIGITS: both NUMERIC FUZZ and NUMERIC DIGITS raise SYNTAX 33.1 for a value that breaks this, and the settings stay as they were.

say fuzz()
numeric fuzz 3
say fuzz() datatype(fuzz(), 'W')
numeric fuzz ' 02.0 '
say fuzz()
numeric fuzz 1e1 - 7
say fuzz()
signal on syntax name a
numeric fuzz 9
a: say condition('o')~code fuzz()
signal on syntax name b
numeric digits 3
b: say condition('o')~code digits() fuzz()

0
3 1
2
3
33.1 3
33.1 9 3
[bif.fuzz.default]

The default of a package is 0 unless a ::OPTIONS directive of the package names another value with its FUZZ keyword. Where it does, that value is the setting at the start of the program, the setting at the start of each of its ::ROUTINE routines and methods, and the setting that the NUMERIC FUZZ instruction without an expression returns to.

say 'start' fuzz()
numeric fuzz 4
say 'set' fuzz()
numeric fuzz
say 'reset' fuzz() later() .holder~new~m
exit
::options fuzz 2
::routine later
numeric fuzz 5
numeric fuzz
return fuzz()
::class holder
::method m
return fuzz()

start 2
set 4
reset 2 2 2
[bif.fuzz.scope]

The setting belongs to the routine or method that is running. An internal routine, which CALL or a function call reaches by its label, starts with the setting in force at the call, and the caller's setting is unchanged when it returns, whatever it set meanwhile. A routine of a ::ROUTINE directive, public or private, a method (also one that another method sends the message to), and an external routine in another file all start with the default of their own package, whatever the setting of the caller. The NUMERIC instruction in an INTERPRET string changes the setting of the running routine, and the change stays after the INTERPRET.

numeric fuzz 2
say 'main' fuzz() inner() later() later2() .holder~new~m
call set4
say 'main' fuzz()
call later3
call hidden
say .holder~new~n
interpret 'numeric fuzz 3'
say 'main' fuzz()
exit
inner: return fuzz()
later: numeric fuzz 1; return fuzz()
set4: numeric fuzz 4; say 'set4' fuzz(); return
::routine later2
return fuzz()
::routine later3
say 'later3' fuzz()
::routine hidden private
say 'hidden' fuzz()
::class holder
::method m
return fuzz()
::method n
numeric fuzz 4
return self~m fuzz()

main 2 2 1 0 0
set4 4
main 2
later3 0
hidden 0
0 4
main 3

GC

GC([force])

rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > GC

GC asks the interpreter to reclaim the storage of objects that the program no longer reaches, and answers whether it did. A program has no need to call it: the interpreter reclaims storage on its own, and a request costs time.

This book does not specify when storage is reclaimed, in what order, or when the UNINIT method of an object runs, whether or not GC is called. A program cannot rely on any of it, and the examples show none of it. What is specified is the argument and the answer.

Arguments

[bif.gc.args]

force is optional. GC does not run as a String method: sending the message GC to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1. The call rules for the number of arguments hold: a second argument raises SYNTAX 40.4, even when the first is omitted. A trailing omitted place adds nothing to the count, so GC(,) is a call without an argument.

signal on syntax name a
say gc(, 'force')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say gc('force', 'force')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say 'force'~gc
c: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say gc(,) == gc()

40.4
40.4
97.1
1
[bif.gc.force]

force is converted to a string and must begin with the letter F, in either case: force, Force, FORCE and f are accepted, and so is any other string whose first character is F or f. Any other value raises SYNTAX 40.904: a string whose first character is something else, a blank or the digit 1 among them, the null string, and an object whose string value starts otherwise, such as .nil or .false. The argument is checked after the count of arguments.

signal on syntax name a
say gc(1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say gc('')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say gc(' force')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say gc(.nil)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say gc(.false)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say gc('x', 'y')
f: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say gc('force') gc('Force') gc('F') gc('f') gc('fx') gc(.mutablebuffer~new('f'))

40.904
40.904
40.904
40.904
40.904
40.4
1 1 1 1 1 1

The result

[bif.gc.answer]

GC answers 1 when it reclaimed storage and 0 when it did not. A call with a valid force always reclaims, and answers 1. A call without force reclaims only on an interpreter built for debugging, which is the case when .RexxInfo~debug is true, and otherwise answers 0; in both cases the answer is the value of .RexxInfo~debug. The answer is the digit alone, 1 or 0, so it can be used as a condition.

say (gc() == .RexxInfo~debug) gc('force') datatype(gc(), 'O')
call gc
r1 = result
call gc 'force'
say (r1 == .RexxInfo~debug) result

1 1 1
1 1
[bif.gc.keeps]

A call changes nothing that the program can see: the variables, stems and objects it holds have the values they had, and the call has no other effect.

a = 'kept'
stem. = 'dflt'
stem.1 = 'one'
o = .array~of('x', 'y')
call gc 'force'
say a stem.1 stem.2 o~items o[2]

kept one dflt 2 y

INSERT

INSERT(new, target [, n [, length [, pad]]])

ANSI: 9.3.11; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > INSERT

Deviations: D4

INSERT puts a string into another string after a given character, adjusting the inserted string to a given length, and answers the combined string.

Arguments

[bif.insert.method]

INSERT is a builtin that runs as a String method, and target, its second argument, is the receiver; new, n, length and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. new and target are strings, n is a whole number of the kind the next rule describes, length is a length, and pad is a pad. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and five is the most.

say insert('123', 'abc', 1) 'abc'~insert('123', 1) '|' 'abc'~insert('123', 1, 2, '.')
signal on syntax name a
say insert('123')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say insert('123', 'abc', 1, 1, '.', 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say insert(, 'abc')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say insert('123', , 1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say insert('123', 'abc', 'x')
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say insert('123', 'abc', 1, 1, '')
f: say condition('o')~code

a123bc a123bc | a12bc
40.3
40.4
40.5
40.5
40.12
40.23
[bif.insert.n.check]

In INSERT, n is a whole-number argument whose value must not be negative. A negative value raises SYNTAX 93.906. An n of 0 is allowed, and so is -0, which is 0. The check is a range check, and falls with those of the conventions, from left to right with the check of length.

say insert('X', 'abc', 0) insert('X', 'abc', '-0')
signal on syntax name a
say insert('X', 'abc', -1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say insert('X', 'abc', -1, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say insert('X', 'abc', 0, -1)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say insert('X', 'abc', -1, 'x')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say insert('X', 'abc', -1, 1, '**')
e: say condition('o')~code

Xabc Xabc
93.906
93.906
93.923
40.12
40.23

Note. A position elsewhere must be positive; n here counts the characters before the insertion, so 0 is its first value.

[bif.insert.n.default]

When n is omitted, it is 0: new goes before the first character of target.

say insert('45', 'xyz') insert('45', 'xyz', ) insert('45', 'xyz', , 1)

45xyz 45xyz 4xyz
[bif.insert.length.default]

When length is omitted, it is the length of new, so new is inserted whole.

say insert('45', 'xyz', 1) insert('', 'xyz', 1) insert('45', 'xyz', 1, )

x45yz xyz x45yz
[bif.insert.pad.default]

When pad is omitted, it is the blank, '20'x.

say '['insert('1', 'abc', 5, 3)']' '['insert('1', 'abc', 5, 3, )']'

[abc  1  ] [abc  1  ]

The result

[bif.insert.result]

INSERT returns the concatenation of three strings, in this order. The first is the first n characters of target, followed by as many copies of pad as it takes to make n characters when target has fewer. The second is new adjusted to exactly length characters: cut at the right when it has more, and followed by copies of pad when it has fewer. The third is the characters of target after position n, which is the null string when target has n characters or fewer. So the length of the result is length plus the larger of n and the length of target.

say insert('45', 'xyz', 3) insert('45', 'xyz', 1, 1) insert('45', 'xyz', 1, 4, '+')
say insert('45', 'xyz', 5, 6, '*') insert('45', 'xyz', , 5, '=')
say '['insert('45', 'xyz', 1, 0)']' insert('1', 'xyz', 4, 3)'.'

xyz45 x4yz x45++yz
xyz**45**** 45===xyz
[xyz] xyz 1  .
[bif.insert.past-end]

When n is greater than the length of target, the gap is filled from target's side: target is extended on the right with copies of pad to n characters, new adjusted to length follows, and nothing follows new. This holds when length is 0, so the result is then target padded to n characters.

say insert('X', 'ab', 4, 1, '.') insert('X', 'ab', 4, 3, '.') insert('xyz', 'ab', 4, 5, '.')
say insert('X', 'ab', 3, 0, '.') insert('X', 'ab', 2, 0, '.')

ab..X ab..X.. ab..xyz..
ab. ab
[bif.insert.empty]

When target is the null string, the first string is n copies of pad and the third is empty, so the result is those copies followed by new adjusted to length. When new is the null string and length is omitted, the result is target padded to n characters, and when length is given the null string new is padded to that length.

say '['insert('X', '', 0)']' '['insert('X', '', 3, 2, '.')']'
say '['insert('', 'ab', 1)']' '['insert('', 'ab', 1, 2, '.')']' '['insert('', '', 3)']'

[X] [...X.]
[ab] [a..b] [   ]
[bif.insert.length.zero]

When length is 0, the second string is the null string, whatever new is: the result is target, padded on the right to n characters when n is more than its length. pad is still checked, as a pad always is.

say '['insert('XYZ', 'ab', 1, 0)']' '['insert('XYZ', 'ab', 5, 0, '.')']'
signal on syntax name a
say insert('XYZ', 'ab', 1, 0, '')
a: say condition('o')~code

[ab] [ab...]
40.23
[bif.insert.bytes]

INSERT cuts and pads by character, one byte each, and copies every byte of new and target that stays unchanged: whitespace, control characters and '00'x are characters like any other, in the strings and as pad.

say c2x(insert('0061'x, '00'x, 1, 3, '00'x)) c2x(insert('c3a9'x, 'ff'x, 0, 1))

00006100 C3FF
[bif.insert.large]

An n or a length that is a whole number below 10**18 is valid, and a value of 10**18 or more raises SYNTAX 40.12 like any whole number that is too large. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS setting plays no part.

signal on syntax name a
say insert('X', 'abc', 1000000000000000000)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say insert('X', 'abc', 1, 1000000000000000000)
b: say condition('o')~code
numeric digits 3
say length(insert('X', 'abc', 1234)) insert('X', 'abcdefghijkl', 1E1)

40.12
40.12
1235 abcdefghijXkl

Note. Whether, when and with which code INSERT fails for an n or a length whose result cannot be held in memory is not specified.

Note. The reference manual says that when n is greater than the length of target, new is padded at the beginning. This page follows ooRexx's behaviour, which pads target as the rule says. The ANSI draft (9.3.11) defines the third string with its SUBSTR, whose count is negative when n is at least LENGTH(target) + 1; read literally it would raise from inside the builtin where this page, like ooRexx, pads (see the note on SUBSTR).

Deviations

[bif.insert.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of INSERT is the same object as another string of equal value: as target itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as insert('', s) does, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'abc'. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'ab' || 'c'
say (insert('', s) == s) (insert('', s, 3, 0) == 'abc')

1 1

LASTPOS

LASTPOS(needle, haystack [, start [, length]])

ANSI: 9.3.12; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > LASTPOS (Last Position)

LASTPOS searches a string for another string, from the end toward the beginning, and answers the position of the first character of the last occurrence, or 0 when there is none. A starting position and a length can confine the search to a stretch of the string. POS searches from the front.

Arguments

[bif.lastpos.method]

LASTPOS is a builtin that runs as a String method, and haystack, its second argument, is the receiver; needle, start and length become the message's arguments, in that order. needle and haystack are strings, start is a position and length is a length. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and four is the most.

say lastpos('/', 'a/b/c') 'a/b/c'~lastpos('/')
signal on syntax name a
say lastpos('a')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say lastpos('a', 'a', 1, 1, 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say lastpos(, 'a')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say lastpos('a', 'a', 0)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say lastpos('a', 'a', 1, -1)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say lastpos('a', 'a', 'x')
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say lastpos('a', 'a', 0, 'x')
g: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name h
say lastpos('a', 'a', 0, -1)
h: say condition('o')~code

4 4
40.3
40.4
40.5
93.924
93.923
40.12
40.12
93.924
[bif.lastpos.start.default]

start is the length of haystack both when it is omitted and when it is greater than that length: the search begins at the last character either way.

say lastpos('a', 'banana') lastpos('a', 'banana', ) lastpos('a', 'banana', 6),
    lastpos('a', 'banana', 7) lastpos('a', 'banana', 999999999999999999)

6 6 6 6 6
[bif.lastpos.length.default]

When length is omitted, the search runs back to the first character of haystack.

say lastpos('b', 'banana', 6) lastpos('b', 'banana', 6, ) lastpos('b', 'banana', 6, 100)

1 1 1

The result

[bif.lastpos.result]

Let n be the length of haystack and m the length of needle. Let e be start, or n when start is omitted or greater than n. The characters that the search covers are those at the positions from e - length + 1 (or from 1, when that is less, or when length is omitted) through e; this is the window, and it holds no characters when length is 0. When m is at least 1, LASTPOS returns the greatest position k such that the m characters of haystack from position k on all lie in the window and are equal under == to needle. When there is no such k, the result is 0. A needle with no characters is the case of its own rule. The answer is written as a count, and whether it is a new object is not specified.

say lastpos('/', 'a/b/c') lastpos('/', 'abc') lastpos('ana', 'banana'),
    lastpos('aa', 'aaa') lastpos('an', 'banana')
numeric digits 3
say lastpos('x', copies('x', 1234) || 'y')

4 0 4 2 4
1234
[bif.lastpos.window]

An occurrence is found only when all of it lies in the window: a start before the end of an occurrence hides it, even when the occurrence begins at or before start, and one that begins before the window is not found. A length that would reach before the first character is cut off there, and start is limited to n before length is applied.

say lastpos('an', 'banana', 5) lastpos('an', 'banana', 4) lastpos('an', 'banana', 3),
    lastpos('an', 'banana', 2)
say lastpos('ana', 'banana', 6, 3) lastpos('ana', 'banana', 6, 2),
    lastpos('ana', 'banana', 5, 3) lastpos('ban', 'banana', 3, 2)
say lastpos('n', 'banana', 4, 2) lastpos('n', 'banana', 4, 1) lastpos('n', 'banana', 6, 3),
    lastpos('b', 'banana', 8, 6) lastpos('a', 'banana', 3, 100)

4 2 2 0
4 0 0 0
3 0 5 1 2
[bif.lastpos.length.zero]

When length is 0, the window holds no characters and the result is 0, for every needle and haystack. -0 is 0.

say lastpos('a', 'banana', 6, 0) lastpos('a', 'banana', , 0),
    lastpos('a', 'banana', 6, '-0')

0 0 0
[bif.lastpos.empty-needle]

When needle has no characters, the result is 0 for every haystack, the null string included. start and length are still checked, as a position and a length always are.

say lastpos('', 'banana') lastpos('', '') lastpos('', 'banana', 3, 2)
signal on syntax name a
say lastpos('', 'banana', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say lastpos('', 'banana', 1, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code

0 0 0
93.924
93.923
[bif.lastpos.empty-haystack]

When haystack is the null string, the result is 0 for every needle and for every start and length that pass their checks.

say lastpos('a', '') lastpos('a', '', 1) lastpos('a', '', 5, 3) lastpos('', '')

0 0 0 0
[bif.lastpos.exact]

Two characters are equal only when they are the same byte. Case matters, whitespace in needle and haystack is compared like any other character, no numeric comparison is made, and '00'x and the other control characters take part like all the rest. A needle longer than haystack is never found, and neither is one that is longer than the window.

say lastpos('A', 'banana') lastpos('a b', 'a b a b') lastpos('a  b', 'a b'),
    lastpos('1', '1 01') lastpos('abc', 'ab') lastpos('ab', 'abab', 3, 2)
say lastpos('00'x, '00'x || 'a' || '00'x || 'b') lastpos('0a'x, '0a'x || 'a')

0 5 0 4 0 0
3 1
[bif.lastpos.string-form]

A needle or haystack that is a number, or an object other than a string, is replaced by its string, and LASTPOS works on the characters of that string as they are written.

say lastpos(1, '1a1') lastpos('.', 3.14) lastpos('an Object', .object~new)

3 2 1

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.12) has no length argument, and defines LASTPOS by comparing the needle with each stretch of the haystack of its length that ends at or before start, working backward. It does not limit start to the length of the haystack: it reads the places past the end as blanks, so a needle of only blanks can be found there. ooRexx limits start first, as this book does.

LEFT

LEFT(string, length [, pad])

ANSI: 9.3.13; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > LEFT

Deviations: D4

LEFT answers the first length characters of a string, adding pad on the right when the string runs out.

Arguments

[bif.left.method]

LEFT is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; length and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. string is a string, length is a length, and pad is a pad. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and three is the most. Unlike SUBSTR, LEFT does not default length: it is a required argument, so a call without it fails by the call rules, with SYNTAX 40.3 when nothing follows its place (too few) and SYNTAX 40.5 when a pad does (missing).

say left('hi yo', 7) '|' 'hi yo'~left(7, '.')
signal on syntax name a
say left('abc')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say left('abc', 2, '.', 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say left('abc', , '.')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say left('abc', 'x')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say left('abc', -1)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say left('abc', 2, '..')
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say left('abc', -1, '..')
g: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name h
say left()
h: say condition('o')~code

hi yo   | hi yo..
40.3
40.4
40.5
40.12
93.923
40.23
40.23
40.3
[bif.left.pad.default]

When pad is omitted, it is the blank, '20'x.

say '['left('ab', 4)']' '['left('ab', 4, )']'

[ab  ] [ab  ]

The result

[bif.left.result]

LEFT returns a string of exactly length characters, the same as SUBSTR(string, 1, length, pad) returns. Its character at position i, for each i from 1 to length, is the character of string at position i when string has one, and pad otherwise. So the result is the first length characters of string, followed by as many copies of pad as make up the length.

say '['left('xy  zw', 5)']' '['left('xy  zw', 9, '.')']' '['left('pq rs', 3)']'
say '['left('abc', 3)']' '['left('abc', 1)']' '['left('abc', 5, '*')']'
say (left('abc', 5, '.') == substr('abc', 1, 5, '.')) (left('abc', 2) == substr('abc', 1, 2))

[xy  z] [xy  zw...] [pq ]
[abc] [a] [abc**]
1 1
[bif.left.length.zero]

When length is 0, the result is the null string, for every string. pad is still checked, as a pad always is.

say '['left('abc', 0)']' '['left('', 0)']' '['left('abc', '-0', '.')']'
signal on syntax name a
say left('abc', 0, '')
a: say condition('o')~code

[] [] []
40.23
[bif.left.empty]

When string is the null string, the result is length copies of pad.

say '['left('', 3)']' '['left('', 3, '*')']'

[   ] [***]
[bif.left.bytes]

LEFT cuts and pads by character, one byte each, and copies every byte of string that stays unchanged: whitespace, control characters and '00'x are characters like any other, in string and as pad.

say c2x(left('0061'x, 4, '00'x)) c2x(left('c3a9'x, 1))

00610000 C3
[bif.left.large]

A length that is a whole number below 10**18 is valid, and a length of 10**18 or more raises SYNTAX 40.12 like any whole number that is too large. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS setting plays no part.

numeric digits 3
say '['left('abc', 1E1)']'
signal on syntax name a
say left('abc', 1000000000000000000)
a: say condition('o')~code

[abc       ]
40.12

Note. Whether, when and with which code LEFT fails for a length whose result cannot be held in memory is not specified.

Deviations

[bif.left.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of LEFT is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as left(s, length(s)) does, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'abc'. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'ab' || 'c'
say (left(s, 3) == s) (left('abcde', 3) == 'abc')

1 1

LENGTH

LENGTH(string)

ANSI: 9.3.14; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > LENGTH

LENGTH answers the number of characters in a string.

Arguments

[bif.length.method]

LENGTH is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its only argument, is the receiver; the message takes no other argument. string is a string, so no string raises an error. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and one is the most.

say length('abc def') 'abc def'~length
signal on syntax name a
say length()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say length('a', 'b')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say length(,)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say length(, 'b')
d: say condition('o')~code

7 7
40.3
40.4
40.3
40.4

The result

[bif.length.result]

LENGTH returns the number of characters in string, which is its length in bytes. The null string has length 0. The answer is written as a count, and whether it is a new object is not specified.

say length('hello') length('hi there') length('')
numeric digits 3
say length(copies('x', 1234))

5 8 0
1234
[bif.length.bytes]

Every character counts once, whatever it is: a blank, a tab, a line feed or '00'x at any place in the string, leading and trailing blanks included, and each byte of what an encoding writes as several.

say length(' ') length(' a  ') length('00'x) length('0a'x || 'b' || '09'x),
    length('c3a9'x)

1 4 1 3 2
[bif.length.string-form]

When string is a number, LENGTH counts the characters of the string the number is, as it is written: a quoted literal keeps its spelling, an unquoted one is a symbol whose exponent letter is E whatever the source wrote, and the result of arithmetic is the string that NUMERIC DIGITS and the arithmetic rules make of it. When string is an object other than a string, it is replaced by its string.

say length(12.00) length(-5) length(1 + 1) length(.object~new)
numeric digits 5
say length(1/3) length(1e20 + 0)
numeric digits 9
say length(1/3)

5 2 1 9
7 5
11

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.14) defines LENGTH as the number of characters in the argument and adds an error for an argument that is not a character string, which cannot occur here: every value is a string.

LINEIN

LINEIN([name] [, [line] [, count]])

ANSI: 9.7.4; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > LINEIN (Line Input)

LINEIN reads a line from a stream and answers it without its line end. It reads from the stream's read position, which a line argument can set first to the start of a given line, and its count of 0 turns the read into a positioning.

Arguments

[bif.linein.args]

name is a string that names the stream; when it is omitted or null, the standard input is read. line is a line number, and count a count: both are whole-number arguments whose value the stream rules give, the line number a valid start. LINEIN is not a String method. It takes three arguments at the most, by the call rules, and none is required.

f = 'spec-linein-args.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'one'
call lineout f, 'two'
call lineout f
say linein(f, 2, ) linein(f, 2, 0)'|' linein(f, 1)
signal on syntax name a
say linein(f, 1, 1, 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say linein(f, 'x')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say linein(f, 0)
c: say condition('o')~code
call sysfiledelete f

two | one
40.4
40.12
93.907
[bif.linein.count]

count is 0 or 1, and 1 when it is omitted. A count of 1 reads a line and a count of 0 reads nothing. A count that is greater than 1 raises SYNTAX 93.0, before the line is checked; a negative count raises SYNTAX 88.907, as the stream rule says.

f = 'spec-linein-count.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'one'
call lineout f
signal on syntax name a
say linein(f, 1, 2)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say linein(f, 0, 2)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say linein(f, 1, -1)
c: say condition('o')~code
say linein(f, , 1) linein(f, 1, '1.0')
call sysfiledelete f

93.0
93.0
88.907
one one

The result

[bif.linein.result]

LINEIN returns the characters from the read position up to the end of the line, without the line end, and moves the read position to the start of the next line. A line of no characters is returned as the null string and raises no condition. A line that ends the data without a line end is returned whole and raises none either; the call after it finds no line.

f = 'spec-linein-result.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'a' || '0a'x || '0a'x || 'c d' || '0d0a'x || 'e' || '0d'x || 'f'
call charout f
n = 0
call on notready name nr
do 4
  x = linein(f)
  say length(x) c2x(x) n
end
x = linein(f)
say length(x) c2x(x) n
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

1 61 0
0  0
3 632064 0
3 650D66 0
0  1

Note. The fourth line is e, a carriage return and f: the carriage return has no line feed after it, so the line does not end there.

[bif.linein.partial]

A line that a read of characters has begun is read from where that read stopped: LINEIN returns the rest of the line, and the read position moves to the start of the next line.

f = 'spec-linein-partial.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'abcdef'
call lineout f, 'ghi'
call lineout f
say charin(f, , 2) linein(f) linein(f)
say charin(f, 9, 1) linein(f)
call sysfiledelete f

ab cdef ghi
h i
[bif.linein.line]

When line is given, LINEIN first sets the read position to the start of line number line, the first line of the stream being line 1, and then reads as it would without it. A line number is counted from the start of the stream, so it names the same line wherever the read position was.

f = 'spec-linein-line.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
do i = 1 to 4
  call lineout f, 'line' i
end
call lineout f
say linein(f, 3) linein(f) linein(f, 1) linein(f, 2)
say linein(f, 4) linein(f, 1)
call sysfiledelete f

line 3 line 4 line 1 line 2
line 4 line 1
[bif.linein.zero]

When count is 0, LINEIN reads nothing and returns the null string. If line is given, it still sets the read position to the start of that line; the next read goes on from there. A line that the stream does not have puts the read position at the end of the data and raises no condition.

f = 'spec-linein-zero.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'ab'
call lineout f, 'cd'
call lineout f, 'ef'
call lineout f
n = 0
call on notready name nr
say '['linein(f, 3, 0)']' charin(f, , 2) '['linein(f, 2, 0)']' linein(f)
say '['linein(f, , 0)']' linein(f)
x = linein(f, 9, 0)
say '[' || x || ']' n chars(f)
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

[] ef [] cd
[] ef
[] 0 0

The end of the data

[bif.linein.end]

When count is 1 and the read position is at the end of the data, or line names a line that the stream does not have, LINEIN returns the null string and raises NOTREADY. The text after a final line end is not a line: line n + 1 of a stream of n lines is such a line number, whether or not the last line has a line end. A stream with no characters has no line. The read position is then at the end of the data.

f = 'spec-linein-end.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'only'
call lineout f
n = 0
call on notready name nr
x = linein(f)
say '[' || x || ']' n
x = linein(f)
say '[' || x || ']' n
x = linein(f, 2)
say '[' || x || ']' n
x = linein(f, 99)
say '[' || x || ']' n chars(f)
x = linein(f, 1)
say '[' || x || ']' n
call charout f
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f
x = linein(f)
say '[' || x || ']' n chars(f)
call charout f
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'p' || '0a'x || 'q'
call charout f
x = linein(f, 3)
say '[' || x || ']' n
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

[only] 0
[] 1
[] 2
[] 3 0
[only] 3
[] 4 0
[] 5
[bif.linein.missing]

A name that cannot be opened for reading, a file that does not exist or a directory for example, has no lines: LINEIN returns the null string and raises NOTREADY, and creates no file. Its line is not checked (see the start rule), but a count that is not valid is.

n = 0
call on notready name nr
x = linein('spec-linein-nofile.tmp')
say '[' || x || ']' n
x = linein('spec-linein-nofile.tmp', 0, 1)
say '[' || x || ']' n
x = linein('.', 1)
say '[' || x || ']' n
say stream('spec-linein-nofile.tmp', 'c', 'query exists') == ''
signal on syntax name a
say linein('spec-linein-nofile.tmp', 1, 2)
a: say condition('o')~code
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

[] 1
[] 2
[] 3
1
93.0
[bif.linein.stdin]

Without a name, LINEIN reads a line of the standard input. At the end of the input it returns the null string and raises NOTREADY.

call on notready name nr
x = linein()
say '[' || x || ']' '[' || linein('', , 0) || ']'
exit
nr: say 'notready' condition('d')
return

notready STDIN
[] []

LINEOUT

LINEOUT([name] [, [string] [, line]])

ANSI: 9.7.5; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > LINEOUT (Line Output)

Deviations: D46, D56, D60

LINEOUT writes a string and a line end to a stream and answers 0 when it did, or 1 when it could not. Given a line number it writes there; given neither a string nor a line number it closes the stream.

Arguments

[bif.lineout.args]

name is a string that names the stream; when it is omitted or null, the standard output is written. string is a string too. line is a line number: a whole-number argument whose value the stream rules give, and a valid start. LINEOUT is not a String method. It takes three arguments at the most, by the call rules, and none is required.

f = 'spec-lineout-args.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
signal on syntax name a
say lineout(f, 'abc', 1, 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say lineout(f, 'abc', 'two')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say lineout(f, 'abc', 0)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say lineout(f, , 0)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say lineout(f, 12, ) lineout(f, 'x', 1.0)
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 9))
call sysfiledelete f

40.4
40.12
93.907
93.907
0 0
780A0A

The result

[bif.lineout.result]

LINEOUT writes the characters of string and then a line end, in order, from the write position, and moves the write position past them. A character written at a position inside the data replaces the one there; a character written after the last one extends the data. The answer is 0 when all of it was written. The line end written is the one the platform uses: on a Unix-like system, a line feed ('0a'x). A string that is the null string writes a line end alone, and a string that holds line ends of its own makes more than one line.

f = 'spec-lineout-result.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
say lineout(f, 'one') lineout(f, '') lineout(f, 12 * 2) lineout(f, 'a' || '0a'x || 'b')
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
say linein(f, 1) '[' || linein(f) || ']' linein(f) linein(f) linein(f)
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

0 0 0 0
6F6E650A0A32340A610A620A
one [] 24 a b

Note. The line end is data of the stream like any other character, and it counts as one however the platform writes it.

[bif.lineout.append]

The write position of a stream just opened is after the last character, so that a LINEOUT without a line adds a line to the end of the data, and the next one adds another after it. When the data ends without a line end, because characters were written to it, LINEOUT continues that last line.

f = 'spec-lineout-append.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'a'
call lineout f
call lineout f, 'b'
call charout f, 'c'
call lineout f, 'd'
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

610A620A63640A

The line argument

[bif.lineout.line]

When line is given, LINEOUT first sets the write position to the start of line number line, the first line of the stream being line 1 and a line being counted by its line end, and then writes as it would without it. A line number is counted from the start of the stream, so it names the same line wherever the write position was. The string replaces characters, not a line: a string that is shorter than the line leaves the rest of its characters where they are, and a longer one overwrites the beginning of the line that follows.

f = 'spec-lineout-line.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'abcdef'
call lineout f, 'ghi'
call lineout f, 'jkl'
call lineout f
call lineout f, 'XY', 1
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call lineout f, 'MNOPQRSTUV', 3
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

58590A6465660A6768690A6A6B6C0A
58590A6465660A4D4E4F505152535455560A

Note. The first write puts XY and a line feed over abc, so that def is now line 2 and ghi line 3. The second write puts its ten letters and a line feed over ghi and jkl and their line ends, and goes on three characters past them.

[bif.lineout.line.end]

A line that is past the last line of the data, one more than the number of lines or more, sets the write position to the end of the data: nothing is filled in, whatever the number. If the last line has no line end, the string therefore continues it. LINEOUT raises no condition for such a line.

f = 'spec-lineout-lineend.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'a'
call lineout f, 'b'
call lineout f
call lineout f, 'c', 3
call lineout f, 'd', 99
call lineout f
call charout f, 'e'
call charout f
call lineout f, 'f', 9
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

610A620A630A640A65660A
[bif.lineout.position-only]

When string is omitted and line is given, LINEOUT writes nothing, sets the write position to the start of that line and answers 0; the next write that gives no line begins there. A string that is the null string is not omitted: it writes a line end at the start of the line.

f = 'spec-lineout-pos.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'abc'
call lineout f, 'def'
call lineout f
say lineout(f, , 2)
call lineout f, 'XYZ'
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call lineout f
say lineout(f, '', 1)
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

0
6162630A58595A0A
0
0A62630A58595A0A
[bif.lineout.close]

When both string and line are omitted, LINEOUT closes the stream and answers 0, as CHAROUT given only a name does. A file that does not exist is created by it, and the characters written are in the file afterwards. A standard stream is closed in the same way, and its next use opens it again, as the lifetime rule says; ooRexx differs (see Deviation 98).

f = 'spec-lineout-close.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
say lineout(f) (stream(f, 'c', 'query exists') \== '') chars(f)
call lineout f, 'abc'
say lineout(f) lineout(f, , ) stream(f)
say chars(f) linein(f)
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

0 1 0
0 0 UNKNOWN
4 abc

When the write fails

[bif.lineout.fail]

When the stream cannot be written, LINEOUT writes nothing, answers 1 and raises NOTREADY. That is the case when the name cannot be opened for writing, as a name in a directory that does not exist, or a directory; when the stream was opened for reading only; and when the name is STDIN and a string is given. For a name that cannot be opened, a line is not checked (see the start rule). What a line does together with the name STDIN is not specified, and so is a call with that name and neither a string nor a line.

f = 'spec-lineout-fail.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
call charout f
n = 0
call on notready name nr
x = lineout('spec-lineout-nodir/x.tmp', 'abc')
say x n
x = lineout('spec-lineout-nodir/x.tmp', , 0)
say x n
x = lineout('.', 'hello')
say x n
x = lineout('stdin', 'q')
say x n
say stream(f, 'c', 'open read')
x = lineout(f, 'q')
say x n left(stream(f, 'd'), 6)
say stream(f, 'c', 'close') chars(f)
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

1 1
1 2
1 3
1 4
READY:
1 5 ERROR:
READY: 3

The standard streams

[bif.lineout.std]

Without a name, LINEOUT writes to the standard output, and with the name STDERR to the standard error. A line for the standard output or the standard error, when it is transient, raises SYNTAX 93.958.

call lineout , 'a'
call lineout 'STDOUT:', 'b'
say lineout(, 'c')
signal on syntax name a
call lineout , 'd', 5
a: say condition('o')~code

a
b

Deviations

[bif.lineout.deviation.46]

On a stream opened BINARY RECLENGTH n, a LINEOUT that only positions, or that closes the stream, clears no record, and only a LINEOUT with a string pads its record. ooRexx clears or pads a record when LINEOUT positions or closes.

f = 'spec-lineout-dev46.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abcdefgh'
call charout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'open binary reclength 4')
say lineout(f, , 1) lineout(f)
say '[' || charin(f, 1, 8) || ']'
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

READY:
0 0
[abcdefgh]
[bif.lineout.deviation.56]

A line counts from the start of the data, as the line rule says, by the line ends that are there, whichever operation touched the stream before. ooRexx counts from a line number that it tracks, which an operation on characters resets: a LINEOUT that gives a line past the last one then writes past the end of the data, and the characters between are '00'x.

f = 'spec-lineout-dev56.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'x'
call lineout f, 'y'
call lineout f, 'z', 2
call charin f, 1, 100
call lineout f, 'z', 3
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

780A7A0A7A0A
[bif.lineout.deviation.60]

A '1a'x at the end of a stream is data like any other character: a write without a line goes after it. ooRexx treats a final '1a'x as the end of the file, and a write there begins at its position.

f = 'spec-lineout-dev60.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab' || '1a'x
call charout f
call lineout f, 'cd'
call lineout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

61621A63640A

LINES

LINES([name] [, option])

ANSI: 9.7.6; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > LINES (Lines Remaining)

Deviations: D54, D58

LINES tells whether a stream has lines left to read, or, when asked, how many. It reads nothing and moves nothing.

Arguments

[bif.lines.args]

name is a string that names the stream; when it is omitted or null, the standard input is asked. option is a string whose first character, in either case, is N or C; the characters after it are ignored. An omitted option is N. An option that is the null string, or begins with any other character, raises SYNTAX 40.904. LINES is not a String method. It takes two arguments at the most, by the call rules, and none is required.

f = 'spec-lines-args.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'a'
call lineout f, 'b'
call lineout f
say lines(f) lines(f, ) lines(f, 'n') lines(f, 'Normal') lines(f, 'c') lines(f, 'Count') lines(f, 'cx')
signal on syntax name a
say lines(f, 'x')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say lines(f, '')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say lines(f, 'N', 1)
c: say condition('o')~code
call sysfiledelete f

1 1 1 1 2 2 2
40.904
40.904
40.4

The result

[bif.lines.normal]

With the option N, LINES answers 1 when a read would find a line, that is when there is a character between the read position and the end of the data, and 0 when there is not. It answers 0 at the end of the data without raising a condition.

f = 'spec-lines-normal.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'a'
call lineout f
say lines(f) linein(f) lines(f)
call charout f, 'xy'
say lines(f) chars(f) charin(f, , 1) lines(f) charin(f, , 1) lines(f) chars(f)
call sysfiledelete f

1 a 0
1 2 x 1 y 0 0

Note. The characters xy were added after the line feed, and so after the read position; LINES counts them at once, like CHARS.

[bif.lines.count]

With the option C, LINES answers the number of lines that the stream has from the read position to the end of the data, the number of line ends there is, plus one when the data ends without a line end after a character. It is the number of calls of LINEIN that find a line. A read position inside a line counts the rest of that line as one. The answer is written as a count, and whether it is a new object is not specified.

f = 'spec-lines-count.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'a' || '0a'x || '0a'x || 'cd' || '0d0a'x || 'ef'
call charout f
say lines(f, 'C')
say linein(f) lines(f, 'C')
say linein(f) lines(f, 'C')
say charin(f, , 1) lines(f, 'C')
say c2x(charin(f, , 3)) lines(f, 'C')
say charin(f, , 1) lines(f, 'C')
say charin(f, 9, 1) lines(f, 'C')
call sysfiledelete f

4
a 3
 2
c 2
640D0A 1
e 1
f 0

Note. After c is read, the rest of its line, d and the line end, still counts as one line, so the count stays 2. The next three characters are d and the two characters of the line end.

[bif.lines.nothing]

LINES neither reads nor moves anything: the read position and the write position are as they were, and the next read starts where it would have started without the call.

f = 'spec-lines-nothing.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'one'
call lineout f, 'two'
call lineout f
say lines(f, 'C') lines(f, 'C') lines(f)
say linein(f) lines(f, 'C') lines(f, 'C') linein(f)
say lines(f, 'C') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
call sysfiledelete f

2 2 1
one 1 1 two
0 9 9

The end of the data

[bif.lines.missing]

A name that cannot be opened for reading, a file that does not exist or a directory for example, has no lines: LINES answers 0, raises NOTREADY and creates no file. LINES raises no condition at the end of the data of a stream that is open.

n = 0
call on notready name nr
x = lines('spec-lines-nofile.tmp')
say x n (stream('spec-lines-nofile.tmp', 'c', 'query exists') == '')
x = lines('spec-lines-nofile.tmp', 'C')
say x n
x = lines('.', 'C')
say x n
f = 'spec-lines-end.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'a'
call charout f
x = charin(f)
x = lines(f)
say x n
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

0 1 1
0 2
0 3
0 3

Deviations

[bif.lines.deviation.54]

LINES of the standard input, or of any other transient stream, answers whether input waits to be read, 0 for none and otherwise a positive number that is not specified, and consumes none. When the input is empty, as it is for the examples of this book, the answer is 0. ooRexx answers 1 to some of these questions when the standard input is /dev/null, which holds no line. For an empty pipe, a pipe that holds data, and a file, it answers as this rule says.

say lines() lines('stdin') lines(, 'C')

0 0 0
[bif.lines.deviation.58]

With the option C, LINES answers the lines that remain after the read position, whatever was done to the stream before. ooRexx's count can be wrong after a character read or a line positioning, and negative.

f = 'spec-lines-dev58.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
do i = 1 to 5
  call lineout f, 'line' i
end
call lineout f
say linein(f, 2) lines(f, 'C')
call charin f, 1, 0
say lines(f, 'C')
call sysfiledelete f

line 2 3
5

LOWER

LOWER(string [, n] [, length])

rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > LOWER

Deviations: D4

LOWER changes the uppercase letters of a string, or of a run of its characters, to lowercase, and leaves every other character as it is. It is the counterpart of UPPER.

Arguments

[bif.lower.method]

LOWER is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; n and length become the message's arguments, in that order. string is a string, n is a position, and length is a length. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: one is required and three is the most.

say lower('Mixed Case') 'Mixed Case'~lower(7)
signal on syntax name a
say lower('ABC', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say lower('ABC', 1, -2)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say lower('ABC', 0, 'two')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say lower('ABC', 1, 1, 1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say lower(, 2)
f: say condition('o')~code

mixed case Mixed case
93.924
93.923
40.12
40.4
40.5
[bif.lower.n.default]

When n is omitted, it is 1: the run starts at the first character of string.

say lower('XYZ', , 2) lower('XYZ', 1, 2)

xyZ xyZ
[bif.lower.length.default]

When length is omitted, the run is every character of string at position n and after it, and no character when n is greater than LENGTH(string).

say lower('UPPER', 3) lower('UPPER', 5) lower('UPPER', 6)

UPper UPPEr UPPER

The result

[bif.lower.case]

Lowercasing changes exactly the 26 characters 'A' to 'Z', '41'x to '5A'x, each to the letter 'a' to 'z' with the same place in the alphabet, '61'x to '7A'x. Every other character is left as it is: the lowercase letters, the digits, whitespace, '00'x, and every character from '80'x to 'FF'x, including the bytes that an encoding such as Latin-1 or UTF-8 uses for an uppercase letter.

say lower('Q-Z 0?_') c2x(lower('C9C3A9DE'x)) c2x(lower('40415a5b'x))
all = xrange('00'x, 'ff'x)
say (lower(all) == translate(all, xrange('a', 'z'), xrange('A', 'Z')))

q-z 0?_ C9C3A9DE 40617A5B
1

Note. The reference manual's LOWER section does not name the characters it changes; this rule is the mirror of the UPPER rule, and ooRexx lowercases exactly those letters. The ANSI draft has no LOWER builtin.

[bif.lower.result]

LOWER returns a string of LENGTH(string) characters. The character at each position from n to n + length - 1 that string has is lowercased, and every other character of string is copied unchanged. A run that reaches past the end of string stops at the end, and nothing is added.

say '['lower('STRING', 2, 3)']' '['lower('STRING', 4, 100)']' '['lower('AB CD')']'

[StriNG] [STRing] [ab cd]
[bif.lower.past-end]

When n is greater than LENGTH(string), no character is changed and the result is string, for every n past the end that passes its check.

say lower('ABC', 4) lower('ABC', 999999999999999999, 2)

ABC ABC
[bif.lower.length.zero]

When length is 0, no character is changed and the result is string, for every n that passes its check.

say lower('ABC', 2, 0) lower('ABC', 50, 0)

ABC ABC
[bif.lower.empty]

When string is the null string, the result is the null string, for every n and length that pass their checks.

say '['lower('')']' '['lower('', 3, 2)']'

[] []

Deviations

Note. An argument whose STRING method answers an object that is not a string falls under Deviation 30, as it does for every builtin.

[bif.lower.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of LOWER is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when no character of it changes, as in lower(s) for an s with no uppercase letter, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'ghij' beside lower('GH' || 'IJ'). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'pq' || 'rs'
say (lower(s) == s) (lower('GH' || 'IJ') == 'ghij')

1 1

MAX(number [, number]...)

MAX answers the greatest of a list of numbers, rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS digits.

Arguments

MAX is a builtin that runs as a String method, and its first number is the receiver; the other numbers become the message's arguments, in their order. The numbers, their checks and the argument count are those of a list of numbers: at least one number is required and there is no most.

say max(3, 8, 5) 3~max(8, 5) '3'~max('8', '5') (3)~max

[bif.max.omitted]

Sent as a message to a receiver that is a number, MAX raises SYNTAX 93.903 when an argument is omitted and a later argument is passed, whether the omitted place is the first argument after the receiver or a later one. Omitted places after the last number passed are no arguments at all. A receiver that is not a number raises SYNTAX 93.943 first. (This is the message form; a function call raises SYNTAX 40.5 for the same mistake, as Deviation 53 says.)

say (4)~max(2,,)

The result

[bif.max.result]

MAX answers the number of the list that no other number of the list is greater than, picked as the list rule says with a later number replacing the candidate when the candidate is less than it. The answer is therefore rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS digits and written in plain or scientific notation, and its sign is kept. A whole number wider than NUMERIC DIGITS is rounded too (see Deviation 44).

say max(15, 4, 8, 11) max(-9, -2, -6.5) max('+2', '1E1', '09')
say max(' 0.0 ', '-0.000') max(-0.5)
numeric digits 3
say max(123456, 5) max(0.01234, 0.01233) max(1000, 999.9)
numeric form engineering

0 -0.5

123E+3 -123E+3
[bif.max.rounding]

The numbers are rounded before they are compared, so two numbers that round to the same value are equal, and MAX answers the earlier of them. This is seen in the written form, which keeps the decimal places of the number picked.

say max(1.00, 1.0004) max(1.0004, 1.00) max(1.0, 1.0004) max(1.0004, 1.0)

1.24 1.24

Numbers that NUMERIC FUZZ makes equal are equal to MAX, which then answers the earlier of them, as the list rule says; whole numbers are no exception (see Deviation 53). With NUMERIC FUZZ 0, the default, only numbers of the same value are equal.

numeric fuzz 1
say max(1.04, 1.01) max(1.01, 1.04) max(1.04, 1.09) max(1.09, 1.04)
say max(1.04, 1.01, 1.09) max(1.09, 1.04, 1.01)
numeric fuzz 0

Deviations

[bif.max.deviation.44]

MAX rounds a whole number to NUMERIC DIGITS digits as it does any other number, in the function form and in the method form, with or without arguments: a whole-number argument wider than NUMERIC DIGITS is rounded before it is compared, and so is the answer. ooRexx answers some such integers unrounded, depending on how the number is held.

numeric digits 3
say max(1, 12345) max(12345, 1) max(5, 12345, 3)

[bif.max.deviation.53]

MAX applies NUMERIC FUZZ to whole numbers as it does to any other numbers, so max(100, 104) answers 100 under NUMERIC DIGITS 3 and NUMERIC FUZZ 1. A function call that omits an argument and passes a later one raises SYNTAX 40.5, whether the omitted argument is the first or a later one; the message form raises SYNTAX 93.903, as its rule says. ooRexx departs from both. It compares some pairs of whole numbers as if NUMERIC FUZZ were 0. Which pairs depends on how each number was written and produced, and on earlier uses of the same string in the program, so the same call can apply FUZZ in one program and not in another. Its function call raises 93.903 when the omitted argument is not the first.

say max(1, , 3)
a: say condition('o')~code

say max(, 3)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
numeric digits 3
numeric fuzz 1
say max(100, 104) max(104, 100) (100)~max(104)

100 104 100

The result

[bif.overlay.result]

OVERLAY returns the concatenation of three strings, in this order. The first is the first n - 1 characters of target, followed by as many copies of pad as it takes to make n - 1 characters when target has fewer. The second is new adjusted to exactly length characters: cut at the right when it has more, and followed by copies of pad when it has fewer. The third is the characters of target from position n + length on, which is the null string when target has fewer than that many characters. So the result keeps every character of target outside the run of length characters from position n, and the result is longer than target when the run reaches past its end.
