40.12
93.923
[bif.space.check-order]

Of the checks that n and pad can fail, the form checks of n and of pad come first, from left to right, and only then the range check of n, as the order of the checks gives: a negative n with a bad pad raises the pad error, and an n that is not a number raises its own error before a bad pad is looked at.

signal on syntax name a
say space('a b', -1, '**')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say space('a b', 'x', '**')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say space('a b', -1, '.')
c: say condition('o')~code

40.23
40.12
93.923

Note. A result of many characters needs memory for them; a request larger than the machine can serve ends in an error that this book does not specify. The ANSI draft (9.3.19) defines SPACE through COPIES and SUBWORD, with the same answers, and checks n for a value below 0 under error 40.13, where ooRexx raises 93.923.

Deviations

Note. An argument whose STRING method answers an object that is not a string falls under Deviation 30, as it does for every builtin.

[bif.space.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of SPACE is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when it is already in the form SPACE gives it, as in space(s) for an s of one blank between each word and none outside, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'x y' beside space('x y'). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'p' || ' ' || 'q'
say (space(s) == s) (space('x  y') == 'x y')

1 1

STREAM

STREAM(name [, operation [, command]])

ANSI: 9.7.8; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > STREAM

Deviations: D34, D35, D49, D55, D57, D59, D62, D74, D79, D98, D100

STREAM asks a stream for its state, describes the state, or carries out a command on the stream: opening and closing it, moving its positions, and asking about the file behind it. The other stream builtins open a stream when they need it, and the program that needs nothing STREAM offers does not call it.

Note. What a command answers about the host, a size or a time or a handle, is the host's. The examples here read back the file they make, and check the shape of an answer where its value belongs to the host.

Arguments

[bif.stream.args]

name is a string that names the stream, and is required: it must be neither omitted nor null. operation is a string that chooses what STREAM does, and command is a string, the command that the operation C carries out. STREAM is not a String method. It takes three arguments at the most, by the call rules. The call is checked in this order. The count of arguments comes first, by the call rules. An omitted name then raises SYNTAX 40.5 and a null one SYNTAX 40.27; an operation that is none of those of the next rule raises SYNTAX 40.904. Last, a command that is missing for the operation C raises SYNTAX 40.3, and a command given for any other operation raises SYNTAX 40.4.

f = 'spec-stream-args.tmp'
do e over "stream()", "stream(,'s')", "stream('','s')", "stream(f,'x')", "stream('','x')",,
          "stream(f,'c')", "stream(f,'s','close')", "stream(f,'d','close')",,
          "stream(f,'c','close','x')", "stream(f,,'close')", "stream(f,'x','close')",,
          "stream(f,'c','query exists')"
  say left(e, 28) '=>' try(e)
end
exit
try: signal on syntax name oops
  interpret 'r =' arg(1)
  return 'no error'
oops: return condition('o')~code

stream()                     => 40.3
stream(,'s')                 => 40.5
stream('','s')               => 40.27
stream(f,'x')                => 40.904
stream('','x')               => 40.27
stream(f,'c')                => 40.3
stream(f,'s','close')        => 40.4
stream(f,'d','close')        => 40.4
stream(f,'c','close','x')    => 40.4
stream(f,,'close')           => 40.4
stream(f,'x','close')        => 40.904
stream(f,'c','query exists') => no error
[bif.stream.operation]

The operation is S for the state of the stream, D for its description and C for a command, and it is the first character of operation, in either case, that decides: the characters after it are ignored. An omitted operation is S.

f = 'spec-stream-op.tmp'
say stream(f) stream(f, ) stream(f, 'S') stream(f, 'state') stream(f, 'Sxyz')
say '['stream(f, 'D')']' '['stream(f, 'description')']' '['stream(f, 'c', 'query exists')']'

UNKNOWN UNKNOWN UNKNOWN UNKNOWN UNKNOWN
[UNKNOWN:] [UNKNOWN:] []

State and description

[bif.stream.state]

The state of a stream is one of four words. UNKNOWN is the state of a stream that is not open. READY is that of an open stream whose last operation went as asked. NOTREADY is that of an open stream whose last read or write could not do all it was asked to, at the end of the data for example. ERROR is that of a stream whose last read or write failed, such as a read of a name that could not be opened, or a write to a stream that was opened for reading only. The state belongs to the one stream: an operation on another changes nothing in it.

a = 'spec-stream-state-a.tmp'
b = 'spec-stream-state-b.tmp'
call sysfiledelete a
call sysfiledelete b
say stream(a) stream(b)
call charout a, 'xy'
call charout b, 'pq'
say stream(a) stream(b)
x = charin(a, 1, 5)
say stream(a) stream(b)
x = charin(b, 1, 1)
say stream(a) stream(b)
say stream('spec-stream-state-none.tmp', 'c', 'open read')
x = charin('spec-stream-state-none.tmp')
say stream('spec-stream-state-none.tmp')
call charout a
call charout b
call sysfiledelete a
call sysfiledelete b

UNKNOWN UNKNOWN
READY READY
NOTREADY READY
NOTREADY READY
ERROR:2
ERROR

Note. The number after ERROR: is the host's number for the failure. It is 2 where a file does not exist, on a Unix-like system. The next rule gives the form.

[bif.stream.change]

Opening a stream, and every read, write, and SEEK or POSITION that succeeds, leave it READY, or NOTREADY when a read or write could not do it all, and a read or write that fails leaves ERROR. CLOSE leaves it UNKNOWN. FLUSH and QUERY leave the state as it was.

f = 'spec-stream-change.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
x = charin(f, 1, 9)
say stream(f) stream(f, 'c', 'query size') stream(f) stream(f, 'c', 'flush') stream(f)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 2') stream(f)
x = charin(f, 1, 1)
say stream(f) stream(f, 'c', 'close') stream(f)
call sysfiledelete f

NOTREADY 3 NOTREADY READY: NOTREADY
2 READY
READY READY: UNKNOWN
[bif.stream.description]

The description of a stream is its state, a colon, and more information about the state when there is any. READY: and UNKNOWN: have none. A stream whose last read stopped at the end of the data is NOTREADY:EOF. A stream in the ERROR state has the host's number for the failure, and may have words after it; in the examples that follow the number is not shown.

f = 'spec-stream-desc.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
say stream(f, 'd')
call charout f, 'ab'
say stream(f, 'd')
x = charin(f, 1, 5)
say stream(f, 'd')
call charout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'open read')
x = charout(f, 'q')
d = stream(f, 'd')
say left(d, 6) datatype(substr(d, 7, 2), 'W')
call charout f
x = charin('spec-stream-desc-none.tmp')
d = stream('spec-stream-desc-none.tmp', 'd')
say left(d, 6) datatype(substr(d, 7, 1), 'W')
call sysfiledelete f

READY:
NOTREADY:EOF
READY:
ERROR: 1
ERROR: 1

Commands

[bif.stream.command]

With the operation C, STREAM carries out command, which begins with a word that names the command: OPEN, CLOSE, FLUSH, SEEK, POSITION or QUERY. The word may be in any case, and may be shortened to any of its leading letters down to the first. What is after the word is the command's own, and the rules for each say what it is. A first word that no command begins with raises SYNTAX 93.914, and anything the command does not take after it, SYNTAX 93.0. A command that is the null string, or only blanks, has no first word, and what it does is not specified.

f = 'spec-stream-command.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 2') stream(f, 'c', 'SEEK 2') stream(f, 'c', 's 2') stream(f, 'c', 'se 2')
say stream(f, 'c', 'position 3') stream(f, 'c', 'p 3') stream(f, 'c', 'f') stream(f, 'c', 'q size')
signal on syntax name a
say stream(f, 'c', 'seeker 2')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say stream(f, 'c', 'flush now')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say stream(f, 'c', 'frobnicate')
c: say condition('o')~code
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f

2 2 2 2
3 3 READY: 3
93.914
93.0
93.914

OPEN

[bif.stream.open.result]

OPEN opens the stream and answers READY:. If it cannot, it answers ERROR: and the host's number for the failure, and raises NOTREADY. A name that is a directory, or is in a directory that does not exist, cannot be opened, and the stream is then not open: its state is UNKNOWN. With no option the stream is opened for reading and writing, and the OPEN of a file that does not allow both fails, where a read alone would open it. A file that does not exist is created by OPEN, unless it is opened for reading only. What follows OPEN is a list of options, the next rules give them. The words SHARED, SHAREREAD, SHAREWRITE and NOBUFFER are accepted, and what they do is not specified; so are their shortenings as far as SHARER, SHAREW and NOB. Any other word in the list raises SYNTAX 93.0, a shortening of SHARED among them.

f = 'spec-stream-open.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
n = 0
call on notready name nr
say stream(f, 'c', 'open read') (stream(f, 'c', 'query exists') == '')
say n
say stream(f, 'c', 'open') (stream(f, 'c', 'query exists') \== '')
say stream(f, 'c', 'close') stream(f, 'c', 'open nobuffer')
say stream(f, 'c', 'close')
say stream('.', 'c', 'open')
say n
say stream('spec-stream-nodir/x.tmp', 'c', 'open write')
say n
say stream('.') stream('spec-stream-nodir/x.tmp')
signal on syntax name a
say stream(f, 'c', 'open reading')
a: say condition('o')~code
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

1

READY: READY:
READY:
ERROR:21

Note. The numbers are those of a Unix-like system: 2 for a file that does not exist, and 21 for a directory. Another host may count differently.

[bif.stream.open.mode]

The options of OPEN say what the stream is for and where it begins. READ opens it for reading only, WRITE for writing only, and BOTH, which is the default, for both. APPEND puts the write position after the last character, which is where a stream that is open for writing and neither APPEND nor REPLACE has it as well, and keeps it there: the write position cannot be moved into the data that the file held when it was opened, by SEEK or by a start or line that a write gives; see Deviation 79. A position at the end of that data, or past it, is allowed, but a write still goes after the last character. On a file that the stream can only write, see Deviation 74. REPLACE empties the file and begins the write position at its start. An option may be shortened as far as to REA, W, BO, AP and REP, and its case does not matter. A word that is given twice, two of READ, WRITE and BOTH, READ with APPEND or REPLACE, and APPEND with REPLACE raise SYNTAX 93.0. A stream for reading only refuses a write: it fails, and the state is ERROR.

f = 'spec-stream-mode.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abcdef'
call charout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'open write') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
say charout(f, 'X') stream(f, 'c', 'close') c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
say stream(f, 'c', 'close')
say stream(f, 'c', 'open both replace') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write') stream(f, 'c', 'query size')
say charout(f, 'YZ') stream(f, 'c', 'close') charin(f, 1, 100)
say stream(f, 'c', 'close')
say stream(f, 'c', 'open read') charout(f, 'Q') left(stream(f, 'd'), 6) charin(f, 1, 1)
say stream(f, 'c', 'close')
say stream(f, 'c', 'open ap') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write') stream(f, 'c', 'close')
say stream(f, 'c', 'open bo rep') stream(f, 'c', 'query size') stream(f, 'c', 'close')
signal on syntax name a
say stream(f, 'c', 'open read replace')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say stream(f, 'c', 'open re')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say stream(f, 'c', 'open write read')
c: say condition('o')~code
call sysfiledelete f

[bif.stream.open.again]

OPEN of a stream that is open opens it afresh: the positions are those of a stream just opened, the read position at the first character and the write position after the last, and the state is READY.

f = 'spec-stream-again.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abcdef'
x = charin(f, , 4)
say stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
say stream(f, 'c', 'open') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')

say stream(f, 'c', 'open') stream(f)

[bif.stream.open.binary]

The option BINARY RECLENGTH n opens the stream as a stream of records of n characters, n being 1 or more: its lines are not delimited by line ends but are consecutive n characters, whatever they are. The words may be shortened as far as to BI and REC. A line end in the data is data. LINEIN answers a record, and the last record may be short. LINES counts records. LINEOUT writes its string and then blanks up to the end of the record that the write position is in, with no line end; a string that is longer than the rest of that record raises SYNTAX 93.0 and writes nothing, and the stream stays READY. The option BINARY without RECLENGTH is not specified, and neither is BINARY RECLENGTH without n.

f = 'spec-stream-binary.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abcdefghij' || '0a'x || 'kl'
call charout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'open binary reclength 4')
say lines(f) lines(f, 'C') chars(f)
say '[' || linein(f) || ']' '[' || linein(f) || ']' c2x(linein(f)) lines(f, 'C')
say '[' || linein(f, 2) || ']' '[' || linein(f, 1) || ']'
call lineout f, 'XY', 2
say stream(f, 'c', 'close')
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call sysfiledelete f

Closing and flushing

[bif.stream.close]

CLOSE closes the stream and answers READY:; its state is then UNKNOWN. The characters written are in the file, and the next use of the name opens the stream afresh. A stream that is not open has nothing to close, and the answer is the null string. A standard stream is closed in the same way: CLOSE of the standard input, output or error answers READY: and leaves its state UNKNOWN, and the next stream builtin that reads from it, writes to it, counts what is left in it (CHARS or LINES) or opens it opens it again on the same input or output, so that later reads and writes carry on, as the lifetime rule says. A QUERY or a FLUSH leaves the state as it was.

f = 'spec-stream-close.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
say '['stream(f, 'c', 'close')']' stream(f)
call charout f, 'abc'
say stream(f) stream(f, 'c', 'close') stream(f) '['stream(f, 'c', 'close')']'
say chars(f) charin(f, , 1)
call charout f
call sysfiledelete f

[] UNKNOWN
READY READY: UNKNOWN []
3 a

say stream('stdin', 'c', 'close') stream('stdin')
say '['linein()']' stream('stdin')

[] NOTREADY
[bif.stream.flush]

FLUSH answers READY:. A file can be asked about, or read back, by the program as it is, whether FLUSH was used or not, so that FLUSH has no other effect that a program can see.

f = 'spec-stream-flush.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
say stream(f, 'c', 'flush') stream(f, 'c', 'query size') stream(f)
call charout f, 'd'
say stream(f, 'c', 'flush') stream(f, 'c', 'query size') chars(f)
call charout f
call sysfiledelete f

READY: 3 READY

Positions

[bif.stream.seek]

SEEK sets a position of the stream and answers the new one. POSITION is the same command. After the word there is an offset, and then options in any order. The offset is a whole number, which may have a prefix: = or no prefix for a position counted from the start of the data, 1 being its first character; < for a position counted back from the end, <0 being the one past the last character; + and - for a position counted forward or back from the read position with READ, and from the write position with WRITE (see Deviation 49). READ sets the read position, WRITE the write position, and when neither is given a stream open for reading and writing has both set to the answer, and a + or - then counts from the read position (see Deviation 49). CHAR counts characters and is the default; for LINE see the next rule. A position past the end of the data is allowed: a read there finds nothing, and a write there fills the gap, except on a stream opened APPEND, where a write goes after the last character wherever the write position is. A stream that is not open is opened by SEEK; when it cannot be, SEEK answers 0, raises NOTREADY, leaves the state ERROR, and creates nothing. An offset that is not a whole number or an option that is not one of these raises SYNTAX 93.0, and a missing offset SYNTAX 93.903.

f = 'spec-stream-seek.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, '0123456789'
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 3') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek =5 read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek +2 read') charin(f, , 1)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek -2 read') charin(f, , 1)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek <2 read') charin(f, , 1)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek <0 read') stream(f, 'c', 'seek <1 write') stream(f, 'c', 'position 4 read')
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek read 4') stream(f, 'c', 'seek char write 6') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 2 write') charout(f, 'W') c2x(charin(f, 1, 10))
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 20 read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') stream(f)
say '[' || charin(f, , 2) || ']'
signal on syntax name a
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek x read')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 2 read write')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek')
c: say condition('o')~code
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f

[bif.stream.seek.line]

With LINE, the offset counts lines and not characters: = counts from the first line, being line 1, and + and - from the line the position is in. The position is set to the start of the line, and the answer is the line number. A line number past the last line sets the position to the end of the data, and the answer is the number of the line that position is in. The prefix < with LINE is not specified. A SEEK by line of a text stream that was opened for writing only answers 0 and raises NOTREADY; see Deviation 55.

call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'ab'
call lineout f, 'cd'
call lineout f, 'ef'
call lineout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek =2 read line') linein(f)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek =3 read line') stream(f, 'c', 'seek -1 read line') linein(f)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek =1 read line') stream(f, 'c', 'seek +2 read line') linein(f)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 9 read line') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') chars(f)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 2 write line') charout(f, 'X') stream(f, 'c', 'close')
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call lineout f
call sysfiledelete f

[bif.stream.query.position]

QUERY POSITION answers the read position of the stream, or, with the option WRITE, the write position, with READ the read position; with no option a stream open for reading and writing answers its read position, and one open for one thing the position that it has. The option CHAR counts characters and is the default; LINE counts lines, and the answer is the number of the line that the position is in. Each option may be shortened to its first letter. The option SYS may be given alone, and what it answers is not specified. A stream that is not open has no positions, and the answer is the null string; so is the answer for a standard stream that is transient (see Deviation 100). On a stream opened APPEND, the write position after a write is just after the last character, wherever the write was asked to go (see Deviation 79).

f = 'spec-stream-qpos.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab' || '0a'x || 'cd' || '0a'x || 'ef'
call charout f

say stream(f, 'c', 'open')
say stream(f, 'c', 'query position') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
x = charin(f, , 4)

say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 1 write') stream(f, 'c', 'q pos w')
say stream(f, 'c', 'close')
say stream(f, 'c', 'open read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position')
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f

Asking about the file

[bif.stream.query.exists]

QUERY EXISTS answers the full name of the file, as QUALIFY makes it (see Deviation 34), if it exists, and the null string if not. A directory is not a file for it, and the answer for one is the null string. It does not create the file, and it does not depend on the stream being open. For a standard stream the answer is its name: STDIN, STDOUT or STDERR.

f = 'spec-stream-exists.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
say '['stream(f, 'c', 'query exists')']' '['stream('.', 'c', 'query exists')']'
call charout f, 'abc'
say stream(f, 'c', 'query exists') == qualify(f)
call charout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'query exists') == qualify(f)
call sysfiledelete f
say '['stream(f, 'c', 'query exists')']'
say stream('stdin', 'c', 'query exists') stream('STDERR:', 'c', 'query exists')

[bif.stream.query.size]

QUERY SIZE answers the number of characters of the file, 0 for an empty file and for a directory, and the null string for a name that is not a file. Characters written are counted at once, whether or not the stream is open.

say stream(f, 'c', 'query size')
call charout f, 'bc'
say stream(f, 'c', 'query size') chars(f)
call charout f
call sysfiledelete f

call charout f, 'a'
say stream(f, 'c', 'query streamtype') stream('stdin', 'c', 'query streamtype')
call charout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'query streamtype')
call sysfiledelete f

[bif.stream.query.time]

QUERY TIMESTAMP answers the date and time that the file was last changed as yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss, and QUERY DATETIME the same moment as mm-dd-yy hh:mm:ss; the null string for a name that is not a file. For a directory they answer its time. They hold the host's time zone, which is not specified.

f = 'spec-stream-time.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
say '['stream(f, 'c', 'query timestamp')']' '['stream(f, 'c', 'query datetime')']'
call charout f, 'a'
call charout f
ts = stream(f, 'c', 'query timestamp')
dt = stream(f, 'c', 'query datetime')
say translate(ts, copies('9', 10), '0123456789') translate(dt, copies('9', 10), '0123456789')
say (substr(dt, 1, 2) == substr(ts, 6, 2)) (substr(dt, 4, 2) == substr(ts, 9, 2)),
    (substr(dt, 7, 2) == substr(ts, 3, 2)) (substr(dt, 10) == substr(ts, 12))
say length(stream('.', 'c', 'query timestamp')) length(stream('.', 'c', 'query datetime'))
call sysfiledelete f

[bif.stream.query.words]

The word after QUERY is EXISTS, SIZE, STREAMTYPE, TIMESTAMP, DATETIME, HANDLE or POSITION, in either case. It may be shortened to any of its leading letters, as far as to its first letter for EXISTS, HANDLE, TIMESTAMP and DATETIME, to SI for SIZE, to ST for STREAMTYPE and to P for POSITION; what a shorter word answers is not specified. A QUERY with no word is not specified. A word that is none of them, and words after it that the query does not take, raise SYNTAX 93.0.

f = 'spec-stream-words.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'

call charout f
call sysfiledelete f

The standard streams

[bif.stream.std]

The standard input, output and error streams are open from the start of the program, and their state is READY. Their names are those of the standard names. The standard input is transient when it is a pipe, and the commands that need positions are not for a transient stream: a SEEK or POSITION of it raises SYNTAX 93.958.

say stream('stdin') stream('STDOUT:') stream('stderr') stream('stdin', 'd')
signal on syntax name a
say stream('stdin', 'c', 'seek 1')
a: say condition('o')~code

READY READY READY READY:
93.958

Deviations

[bif.stream.deviation.34]

In a stream's name, as in every name interrexx qualifies, each .. removes exactly the one component before it, however the component was written, so .b/../c names the file c beside the directory .b. ooRexx removes none after a doubled slash and two after a component that starts with a period, so its stream can be a different file.

address system 'mktemp -d' with output stem t.
base = t.1
call sysmkdir base || '/.b'
f = base || '/c'
call charout f, 'abc'
call charout f
g = base || '/.b/../c'
say (stream(g, 'c', 'query exists') == f) chars(g) charin(g, 1, 3)
call stream g, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f
call sysrmdir base || '/.b'
call sysrmdir base

1 3 abc
[bif.stream.deviation.35]

The names HANDLE:0, HANDLE:1 and HANDLE:2 denote the standard input, output and error streams, and read and write them; a HANDLE: stream with any other descriptor is refused when it is created. In ooRexx a HANDLE: stream never reaches its descriptor: reads see end of file, and writes crash.

call charout 'HANDLE:1', 'hello '
call charout 'handle:1', 'again'
say
say stream('HANDLE:1') '['charin('HANDLE:0')']'

hello again
READY []
[bif.stream.deviation.49]

On a stream open for reading and writing, a relative SEEK with READ moves from the read position, and one with WRITE from the write position, whatever operation came before. One with neither option moves from the read position. ooRexx counts from a position that it tracks, which can be the other one: with neither option, the position that the last read, write or SEEK used, and the write position when there has been none since the stream was opened.

f = 'spec-stream-dev49.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'ab'
call lineout f, 'cd'
call lineout f, 'ef'
call lineout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'open')
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek +1 read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read')
say stream(f, 'c', 'open')
x = charin(f, , 3)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek +1 write') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read')
say stream(f, 'c', 'open')
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek +2') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
x = charin(f, , 2)
call charout f, 'X'
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek -1') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f

READY:

READY:
3 3
4 4
[bif.stream.deviation.55]

A stream opened WRITE reads nothing: a read fails and the state is ERROR, CHARS and LINES answer 0, and positioning by line is NOTREADY: a SEEK by line answers 0 and a LINEOUT that gives a line answers 1. ooRexx opens it for reading and writing.

f = 'spec-stream-dev55.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab' || '0a'x || 'cd'
call charout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'open write')
x = charin(f, 1, 1)
say '[' || x || ']' stream(f) chars(f) lines(f) lines(f, 'C')
n = 0
call on notready name nr
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 1 write line')
say n
say lineout(f, 'M', 1)
say n
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

QUERY POSITION ... LINE answers the line that the position is in, and 0 for the write position of a stream open for reading only. ooRexx answers a line number it tracks.

[bif.stream.deviation.59]

A SEEK or POSITION to a position below 1 answers 0, raises NOTREADY and moves nothing; so does one of the write position of a stream open for reading only. ooRexx answers a position it has not checked.

f = 'spec-stream-dev59.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
call charout f
say stream(f, 'c', 'open read')
n = 0
call on notready name nr
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 0 read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') n
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek -9 read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read') n
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 2 write') n
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

0 1 0

[bif.stream.deviation.62]

A read that finds nothing at the end of the data leaves the stream NOTREADY with the description NOTREADY:EOF. ooRexx leaves ERROR:0 after a CHARIN of nothing.

f = 'spec-stream-dev62.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab'
call charout f
x = charin(f, 1, 2)
say stream(f, 'd')
x = charin(f, , 1)
say stream(f, 'd')
call charout f
call sysfiledelete f

READY:
NOTREADY:EOF
[bif.stream.deviation.74]

A stream opened APPEND on a file it can only write writes every line at the file's current end, after what another writer appended since the stream was opened. ooRexx writes at the end as it was when the stream was opened, overwriting what another writer appended meanwhile.

f = 'spec-stream-dev74.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'one'
call lineout f
address system 'chmod 200' f
call stream f, 'c', 'open write append'
address system 'printf "two\n" >>' f
call lineout f, 'three'
call lineout f
address system 'chmod 600' f
do while lines(f) > 0
  say linein(f)
end
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f

one
two
three
[bif.stream.deviation.79]

On a stream opened APPEND, every write goes after the last character, wherever the write position has been set: a position past the end leaves no gap, and a position in data written since the stream was opened does not overwrite it. The write position cannot be moved into the data that the file held when it was opened: a SEEK of it there answers 0, and a CHAROUT or LINEOUT that names a position there writes nothing, all of them NOTREADY. After a write, the write position is just after the last character, wherever the write was asked to go. ooRexx differs there: it moves the position, and the write goes after the last character as any other does; the write position it reports afterwards is the one that a CHAROUT start named, or that a SEEK set, moved past the characters written.

f = 'spec-stream-dev79.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abcdefgh'
call charout f
n = 0
call on notready name nr
say stream(f, 'c', 'open append')
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 2 write')
say n stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
say charout(f, 'Y', 1)
say n
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 9 write') charout(f, 'Z', 9)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 20 write') charout(f, 'W') charout(f, 'V', 10) n
say stream(f, 'c', 'query position write') charout(f, 'U', 100),
    stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
say charin(f, 1, 100)
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

READY:
0
1 9
1
2
9 0
20 0 0 2
12 0 13
abcdefghZWVU
[bif.stream.deviation.98]

CLOSE of the standard output or error closes it as it closes any stream, and the output written after it appears. In ooRexx, that output does not appear at once: it appears when the program next closes, flushes or opens the stream, and what is written after the last of these is lost. Deviation 98 gives the whole of the difference.

say 'one'
r = stream('stdout', 'c', 'close')
s = stream('stdout')
call lineout 'stdout', r s
say 'two' stream('stdout')

one
READY: UNKNOWN
two READY
[bif.stream.deviation.100]

QUERY POSITION of a standard stream that is transient answers the null string, with any option, because a transient stream has no position. ooRexx answers 1.

say '[' || stream('stdin', 'c', 'query position') || ']',
    '[' || stream('stdout', 'c', 'query position write') || ']',
    '[' || stream('stderr', 'c', 'query position read line') || ']'

STRIP

STRIP(string [, option] [, chars])

ANSI: 9.3.20; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > STRIP

Deviations: D4

STRIP removes characters from the start of a string, from its end, or from both, for as long as they belong to a set of unwanted characters. By default that set is the whitespace.

Arguments

[bif.strip.method]

STRIP is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; option and chars become the message's arguments, in that order. string and chars are strings, and option is an option. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and three is the most.

x = ' pq '~strip('t')
say '['strip('   mn   ')']' '[' || x || ']'
signal on syntax name a
say strip('ab', 'Q')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say strip('ab', , 'a', 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say strip(, 'L')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say strip()
d: say condition('o')~code

[mn] [ pq]
93.915
40.4
40.5
40.3
[bif.strip.option]

option selects the end or ends of string that are stripped, by its first character alone, in either case: L or l selects the leading end, T or t the trailing end, and B or b both. Only that character decides; option may go on with any characters, and they change nothing. When option is omitted, it is B.

say '['strip(' k  l ', 'l')']' '['strip(' k  l ', 'T')']' '['strip(' k  l ')']'
say '['strip('  a  ', 'Leading')']' '['strip('  a  ', 'trailing')']',
    '['strip('  a  ', 'Both')']'
say '['strip('  a  ', 'lx')']' '['strip('  a  ', , )']'

[k  l ] [ k  l] [k  l]
[a  ] [  a] [a]
[a  ] [a]
[bif.strip.option.check]

An option whose first character is not one of those six, and an option that is the null string, raise SYNTAX 93.915. No other argument has a check, so this is the only check STRIP makes of its own after the argument count, and it is made whatever string and chars are.

signal on syntax name a
say strip('ab', 'X')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say strip('ab', '')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say strip('ab', ' L')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say strip('', 'Y')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say strip('ab', 1, 'ab')
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say strip(, 'Y')
g: say condition('o')~code

93.915
93.915
93.915
93.915
40.5

Note. The reference manual names error 93.915 for a method option that is not one of those allowed. The ANSI draft (9.3.20) reads option the same way, by its first character in either case, but raises 40.21 for a null option and 40.28 for any other bad one, where ooRexx raises 93.915; and it makes chars one character, where ooRexx takes the characters of chars as a set, as the rule below says.

[bif.strip.chars]

chars is the set of unwanted characters: the characters it holds, in any order and whether or not one repeats. When chars is omitted, the set is the two whitespace characters, the blank and the tab. Case matters: a is not A. Any character may be in the set, '00'x and those from '80'x to 'FF'x included.

say '['strip('xyxaxyb', , 'xy')']' '['strip('A a A', , 'a')']'
say c2x(strip('00'x || 'a' || '00'x, , '00'x)) c2x(strip('80'x || 'a' || '81'x, , '81'x))
say c2x(strip('09'x || ' a' || '09'x)) c2x(strip('0a'x || 'a' || '0d'x))
say c2x(strip('0b'x || 'a' || '0c'x)) c2x(strip('09'x || ' a ' || '09'x, , ' '))

[axyb] [A a A]
61 8061
61 0A610D
0B610C 0920612009

The result

[bif.strip.result]

STRIP returns string with the run that option selects removed: the run at its start, the run at its end, or both. The leading characters removed are the longest run at the start of string made of characters in the set, and the trailing ones the longest such run at the end. Characters between them are not touched, whether or not they are in the set. A character of the set that is not in such a run, because a character outside the set stands between it and the end, stays.

say '['strip('xxaxbxx', 'L', 'x')']' '['strip('xxaxbxx', 'T', 'x')']',
    '['strip('xxaxbxx', 'B', 'x')']'
say '['strip('abcba', 'L', 'ba')']' '['strip('abcba', , 'ba')']' '['strip('  a b  ')']'
say c2x(strip(' ' || '09'x || 'a', , ' '))

[axbxx] [xxaxb] [axb]
[cba] [c] [a b]
0961
[bif.strip.all]

When every character of string is in the set, the result is the null string, whichever option is. The null string strips to the null string.

say '['strip('xxx', 'L', 'x')']' '['strip('xxx', 'T', 'x')']' '['strip('xxx', , 'x')']'
say '['strip('')']' '['strip('  ' || '09'x)']' '['strip('', , 'x')']'

[] [] []
[] [] []
[bif.strip.chars.null]

A null chars is an empty set, so STRIP removes nothing and returns string, for every option. A null chars is not omitted, so it does not give the default set.

say '['strip('  a  ', , '')']' '['strip('  a  ', 'L', '')']',
    '['strip('  a  ', 'T', '')']'

[  a  ] [  a  ] [  a  ]
[bif.strip.omitted-chars]

An omitted chars takes the default set, an omitted option takes B, and the two are independent of each other.

say '['strip('  a  ', 'L', )']' '['strip('  a  ', , )']' '['strip('xxaxx', , 'x')']'

[a  ] [a] [a]

Deviations

Note. An argument whose STRING method answers an object that is not a string falls under Deviation 30, as it does for every builtin.

[bif.strip.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of STRIP is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when nothing is stripped, as in strip(s) for an s with no whitespace at either end, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'ab' beside strip(' ab'). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'p' || 'q'
say (strip(s) == s) (strip('  ab') == 'ab')

SUBSTR

SUBSTR(string, n [, length] [, pad])

ANSI: 9.3.21; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > SUBSTR (Substring)

Deviations: D4

SUBSTR selects a run of characters from a string by position, and pads the run when it reaches past the end of the string.

Arguments

[bif.substr.method]

SUBSTR is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver. string is a string, n is a position, length is a length, and pad is a pad. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and four is the most.

signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', 2, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say substr('abc', 1, 2, '..')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say substr('abc', 1, 1, '.', 1)
d: say condition('o')~code

93.924
93.923
40.23
40.4
[bif.substr.length.default]

When length is omitted, it is the number of characters of string at position n and after it: LENGTH(string) - n + 1 when n is at most LENGTH(string), and 0 otherwise.

say '['substr('abcde', 2)']' '['substr('abcde', 5)']',
    '['substr('abcde', 6)']' '['substr('abcde', 100)']'

[bcde] [e] [] []

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.21) computes the omitted length as LENGTH(string) + 1 - n and repeats that many times, so for n two or more past the end its count is negative and its definition raises SYNTAX 26.2 from inside the builtin. This page follows ooRexx, where the reference manual says the rest of the string is returned and positions past the end select nothing, so the result is the null string.

[bif.substr.pad.default]

When pad is omitted, it is the blank, '20'x.

say '['substr('xyz', 3, 3)']'

[z  ]

The result

[bif.substr.result]

SUBSTR returns a string of exactly length characters. Its character at position i, for each i from 1 to length, is the character of string at position n + i - 1 when string has a character there, and pad otherwise. So the result is the characters of string from position n on, at most length of them, followed by as many copies of pad as make up the length.

say '['substr('abcdef', 2, 3)']' '['substr('abcdef', 4, 5, '.')']',
    '['substr('abcdef', 1, 6)']'

[bcd] [def..] [abcdef]
[bif.substr.past-end]

When n is greater than LENGTH(string), no character of string is selected: the result is length copies of pad, and the null string when length is omitted. This holds for every n past the end that passes its check.

say '['substr('abc', 4, 2, '*')']' '['substr('abc', 999999999999999999, 3, '*')']',
    '['substr('abc', 4)']'

[**] [***] []
[bif.substr.length.zero]

When length is 0, the result is the null string, for every n that passes its check. pad is still checked, as a pad always is.

say '['substr('abc', 2, 0)']' '['substr('abc', 10, 0, '*')']'
signal on syntax name e
say substr('abc', 2, 0, '')
e: say condition('o')~code

[] []
40.23
[bif.substr.empty]

When string is the null string, every position is past its end, so the result is length copies of pad, or the null string when length is omitted.

say '['substr('', 1)']' '['substr('', 1, 3)']' '['substr('', 5, 2, '-')']'

[] [   ] [--]
[bif.substr.bytes]

SUBSTR selects and pads by character, one byte each, and copies every byte unchanged: whitespace, control characters and '00'x are characters like any other, in string and as pad.

say c2x(substr('61000962'x, 2, 4, '00'x))

00096200

Deviations

[bif.substr.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of SUBSTR is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as substr(s, 1) does, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'abc' beside substr('abcdef', 1, 3). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'abc' || 'def'
say (substr(s, 1) == s) (substr('abcdef', 1, 3) == 'abc')

SUBWORD

SUBWORD(string, n [, length])

ANSI: 9.3.22; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > SUBWORD

Deviations: D4

SUBWORD selects a run of consecutive words from a string, keeping the whitespace between them as it is. Words are those of the word rule.

Arguments

[bif.subword.method]

SUBWORD is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver. string is a string, n is a word number, and length is a length that counts words. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and three is the most.

signal on syntax name a
say subword('a b', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say subword('a b', 1, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say subword('a b', 0, 'x')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say subword('a b', 1, 1, 1)
d: say condition('o')~code

93.924
93.923
40.12
40.4
[bif.subword.length.default]

When length is omitted, it selects every word from word n to the last word of string.

say '['subword('one two  three', 2)']' '['subword('one two  three', 3)']'

[two  three] [three]

The result

[bif.subword.result]

When string has a word n and length is not 0, SUBWORD returns the part of string that begins with the first character of word n and ends with the last character of word n + length - 1, or of the last word of string when it has fewer words than that. It is a slice of string and nothing is rewritten in it, so a run of blanks or tabs separating two selected words keeps its length and its characters. Since the slice starts and ends on word characters, whitespace before word n, and after the last selected word, falls outside it. The other cases have rules of their own: n past the last word, length 0 and a string with no words.

say '['subword('one two  three   four', 2, 2)']'
say '['subword('  one  two  ', 1)']' '['subword('a b c', 2, 100)']'
say c2x(subword('09'x||'a'||'0909'x||'b'||'09'x, 1))

[two  three]
[one  two] [b c]
61090962
[bif.subword.past-end]

When n is greater than the number of words in string, the result is the null string. This holds for every n past the last word that passes its check.

say '['subword('a b c', 4)']' '['subword('a b c', 999999999999999999, 2)']'

[] []
[bif.subword.length.zero]

When length is 0, the result is the null string, for every n that passes its check.

say '['subword('a b c', 2, 0)']' '['subword('a b c', 9, 0)']'

[] []
[bif.subword.empty]

When string has no words, the null string or a string of only whitespace among them, the result is the null string for every n and length that pass their checks.

say '['subword('', 1)']' '['subword(' '||'09'x||' ', 1, 2)']'

[] []
[bif.subword.nonblank]

A character that the word rule places inside a word, such as a line feed or a carriage return, is copied into the result as it stands, and SUBWORD ends the result after it when it is the last character of the last selected word.

say c2x(subword('a'||'0a'x||'b c', 1, 1)) c2x(subword('a'||'0d'x||' b', 1, 1))

610A62 610D

Deviations

[bif.subword.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of SUBWORD is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as subword(w, 1) does for a w with no whitespace around its words, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'a b' beside subword('a b c', 1, 2). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

w = 'a' || ' b'
say (subword(w, 1) == w) (subword('a b c', 1, 2) == 'a b')

1 1

SYMBOL

SYMBOL(name)

ANSI: 9.8.4; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > SYMBOL

SYMBOL tells whether a string is a symbol and, if so, whether a variable of that name holds a value where SYMBOL is called. The answer is one of the three strings BAD, VAR and LIT.

Arguments

[bif.symbol.args]

SYMBOL takes one argument, name, which is a string, and nothing else. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one argument is required and one is the most. SYMBOL does not run as a String method: sending the message SYMBOL to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

signal on syntax name a
say symbol()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say symbol('a', 'b')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say symbol(, )
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say 'a'~symbol
d: say condition('o')~code

40.3
40.4
40.3
97.1

The result

[bif.symbol.result]

The answer is BAD when name is not a symbol, VAR when it is a symbol that names a variable holding a value, and LIT for any other symbol. A string is a symbol when it has at least one character and each is a letter, a digit, or one of ., !, ? and _, as it is for the symbol type of DATATYPE, and it has at most 250 characters; the null string, a string with whitespace anywhere in it, even at an end, one with any other character, and one of more than 250 characters, whatever they are, is BAD. The string is read as it is, without trimming. A name that is an object other than a string is replaced by a string as any string argument says.

n = 7
say symbol('n') symbol('p') symbol('a_b') symbol('a!') symbol('a?') symbol('_')
say symbol('') symbol(' j') symbol('j ') symbol('a b') symbol('+5') symbol('a-b'),
    symbol('a$') symbol('"j"') symbol('é')
say symbol(.nil) symbol(.array~new) symbol(.mutablebuffer~new('n'))
say symbol(copies('a', 250)) symbol(copies('a', 251)) symbol(copies('1', 251)),
    symbol(copies('a', 100)'.'copies('b', 149)) symbol(copies('a', 100)'.'copies('b', 150))

VAR LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT
BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD
BAD BAD VAR
LIT BAD BAD LIT BAD

Note. The limit of 250 is on the whole string, stem and tail together.

[bif.symbol.case]

SYMBOL reads name in uppercase, as a program reads a symbol, so name names the same variable in either case.

n = 7
say symbol('n') symbol('N') symbol('p') symbol('P')

VAR VAR LIT LIT
[bif.symbol.constant]

A symbol that starts with a digit or a period is a constant symbol and is never a variable, so SYMBOL answers LIT for it. The name .nil and the other names that stand for environment objects are of this kind, whether or not the object exists.

say symbol('3') symbol('1.5') symbol('.5') symbol('1e5') symbol('.') symbol('..'),
    symbol('.nil') symbol('.zzz')

LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT
[bif.symbol.simple]

For any other symbol without a period inside it, SYMBOL answers VAR when a variable of that name holds a value and LIT when it does not. A variable that has been dropped holds no value. SYMBOL looks at the name itself, not at the value: a variable whose value is the name of another variable makes the answer for the name VAR, and the answer for the value is a separate one that the call gets when it is given the value.

a = 'b'
b = 'c'
say symbol('a') symbol('b') symbol('c') symbol(a) symbol(b)
drop a
say symbol('a')

VAR VAR LIT VAR LIT
LIT
[bif.symbol.compound]

A symbol whose first period has at least one character after it, and that does not start with a period, is a compound symbol: the part before the first period is its stem, and the parts after it are its tail, so a.b. is a compound symbol with the tail b.. Every part of the tail that names a variable holding a value is replaced by that value, as in a program, and the answer is VAR when the compound variable so named holds a value, and LIT when it does not. The value of a tail part is used as it is, not translated to uppercase, and can be any string, whitespace included; it is not itself checked to be a symbol. An unset part of the tail stands for its own name in uppercase.

n = 7
t.7 = 'x'
say symbol('t.7') symbol('t.n') symbol('T.N') symbol('t.8') symbol('t.m')
drop n
say symbol('n') symbol('t.n') symbol('t.7')
w = 'x y'
c.w = 1
say symbol('c.w') symbol('c.x y')
v = 'k'
d.k = 1
say symbol('d.v') symbol('d.k') symbol('d.K')
e.f. = 1
say symbol('e.f.') symbol('e.f')

VAR VAR VAR LIT LIT
LIT LIT VAR
VAR BAD
LIT VAR VAR
VAR LIT
[bif.symbol.stem]

A symbol that ends at its first period is a stem. A stem is LIT until the program refers to the stem or to a compound variable of it, and VAR from then on, also after the stem is dropped. A reference is an assignment, a read, a DROP of the stem or of a compound variable of it, or a call of SYMBOL that names a compound variable of it; a call that names the stem itself is not a reference. After an assignment to the whole stem, a compound variable of it that was never assigned or dropped is VAR, because it has the value given to the stem. A compound variable that was dropped, and every compound variable of a dropped stem, holds no value and is LIT.

say symbol('a.')
say symbol('b.1') symbol('b.')
stem. = 0
say symbol('stem.') symbol('stem.zzz') symbol('other.')
h. = 0
drop h.1
say symbol('h.') symbol('h.1') symbol('h.2')
c.1 = 5
drop c.
say symbol('c.') symbol('c.1')
d = e.1
say symbol('e.')

LIT
LIT VAR
VAR VAR LIT
VAR LIT VAR
VAR LIT
VAR

Note. In the second line the call that names b.1 is a reference to b., which the call after it sees; the same two calls in the other order answer LIT LIT.

Scope

[bif.symbol.scope]

SYMBOL looks at the variables that the routine or method running it can see. A routine called with a PROCEDURE instruction sees none of its caller's variables, except the ones it EXPOSEs; a method sees an object variable only once it exposes it, and the variable is VAR only when it holds a value.

g = 1
call hide
call show
exit
hide: procedure
say symbol('g')
return
show: procedure expose g
say symbol('g')
return

LIT
VAR

o = .o~new
say o~plain '/' o~exposing '/' o~assigning '/' o~exposing
::class o
::attribute at
::method plain
return symbol('at') symbol('un')
::method exposing
expose at un
return symbol('at') symbol('un')
::method assigning
expose at
at = 1
return symbol('at')

LIT LIT / LIT LIT / VAR / VAR LIT
[bif.symbol.result-var]

The variable RESULT is VAR after a CALL of a routine that returned a value and LIT after a CALL of one that returned none, as the instruction sets or drops it.

call none
say symbol('result')
call one
say symbol('result')
call none
say symbol('result')
exit
none: return
one: return 1

LIT
VAR
LIT

TIME

TIME([option [, [string] [, informat]]])

ANSI: 9.8.5; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > TIME

TIME answers a time of day. With no string it answers the current local time, or the reading of an elapsed-time clock that the program can start and reset; with a string it reads a time written in one format and writes it in another. The current time changes from moment to moment, so the examples of this page convert fixed times, or check only the form of the current time and how its formats agree with each other, and the elapsed-time clock is checked against pauses and not against figures.

Arguments

[bif.time.args]

TIME takes up to three arguments and requires none: option, string and informat. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: a call with more than three arguments raises SYNTAX 40.4, and a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments. TIME does not run as a String method: sending the message TIME to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1. option and informat name formats by their first letter.

say time('C', '13:05:09') time(, '13:05:09') time('N', '13:05:09', 'N') time('N', '13:05:09', )
signal on syntax name a
say time('N', '13:05:09', 'N', 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say '13:05:09'~time
b: say condition('o')~code

1:05pm 13:05:09 13:05:09 13:05:09
40.4
97.1
[bif.time.default]

An omitted option is N, and so is an omitted informat. A call with no string answers the current time, in the format option names; a call with a string is a conversion.

say time(, '07:08:09') time('N', '07:08:09') time(, '07:08:09', 'N')
say (time() == time('N')) (length(time()) == 8)

07:08:09 07:08:09 07:08:09
1 1

Formats written

[bif.time.out.clock]

Three options write the time of day as hours, minutes and seconds. N writes hh:mm:ss, with the hour from 00 to 23, and L writes hh:mm:ss.uuuuuu, which adds six digits for the microseconds. C writes h:mmam or h:mmpm, a civil time: the hour is from 1 to 12 with no leading zero, the minutes have two digits and the seconds are not written. The hour 0 is 12 with am, the hours 1 to 11 have am, the hour 12 is 12 with pm, and the hours 13 to 23 are 1 to 11 with pm.

say time('N', '00:00:00') time('N', '09:08:07') time('N', '23:59:59')
say time('L', '09:08:07') time('L', '09:08:07.5', 'L') time('L', '23:59:59.999999', 'L')
say time('C', '00:00:00') time('C', '00:59:59') time('C', '01:00:00') time('C', '11:59:59')
say time('C', '12:00:00') time('C', '12:59:59') time('C', '13:00:00') time('C', '23:59:59')

00:00:00 09:08:07 23:59:59
09:08:07.000000 09:08:07.500000 23:59:59.999999
12:00am 12:59am 1:00am 11:59am
12:00pm 12:59pm 1:00pm 11:59pm
[bif.time.out.counts]

Three options write the time of day as a count since midnight: H the whole hours, M the whole minutes and S the whole seconds. Each is written with no leading zero, point or exponent, as 0 for zero, and a part of a unit that is not complete is dropped, never rounded. NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part.

numeric digits 2
say time('H', '00:00:00') time('H', '09:59:59') time('H', '23:59:59')
say time('M', '00:00:59') time('M', '01:00:00') time('M', '23:59:59')
say time('S', '00:00:01') time('S', '01:00:00') time('S', '23:59:59')

0 9 23
0 60 1439
1 3600 86399
[bif.time.out.stamp]

Two options write a count that includes the date. F writes the number of microseconds since the start of 1 January 0001, and T the number of seconds since the start of 1 January 1970, which is negative before it. T is F divided by 1000000, rounded down, less 62135596800. A string read with the informat C, H, L, M, N or S has no date, so its date is 1 January 0001: F is then the time of day in microseconds, and T is that time of day in seconds less 62135596800, a negative number. NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part in how they are written.

say time('F', '00:00:00') time('F', '00:00:01') time('F', '23:59:59.999999', 'L')
say time('T', '00:00:00') time('T', '00:00:01') time('T', '23:59:59.999999', 'L')
numeric digits 3
say time('F', '13:05:09') time('T', '13:05:09')
say time('F', '13:05:09') + 0

0 1000000 86399999999
-62135596800 -62135596799 -62135510401
47109000000 -62135549691
4.71E+10

The current time

[bif.time.current]

A call with no string answers the current time in the local time zone, in the format option names, as of the moment the clause reads the clock. Every format of the current time is the same time: converting the current time in L form to N, C, H, M, S or L gives what that option gives for the current time. F and T include the date, and F with its whole days taken off is what the conversion of the L form gives for F.

numeric digits 20
say (time('N') == time('N', time('L'), 'L')) (time('C') == time('C', time('L'), 'L')),
    (time('H') == time('H', time('L'), 'L')) (time('M') == time('M', time('L'), 'L')),
    (time('S') == time('S', time('L'), 'L')) (time('L') == time('L', time('L'), 'L'))
say (time('F') // 86400000000 == time('F', time('L'), 'L')),
    (time('T') == date('T'))
say length(time('L')) length(time('N')) datatype(time('S'), 'W') datatype(time('F'), 'W') datatype(time('T'), 'W')

1 1 1 1 1 1
1 1
15 8 1 1 1

The time zone

[bif.time.zone]

The current time of every format is that of the local time zone, and the option O writes how far that zone is from UTC: a whole number of microseconds, positive east of UTC and negative to the west, and less than a day. F and T are local like the rest: the UTC reading of F is F - O. A call that gives O with a string reads the string as usual and answers the same offset, except with the informat O, whose answer is the offset that the string gives. This book does not specify which time zone a program runs in. The zone is read with the clock, at the clause's moment. A program that changes it, as by setting TZ with VALUE in the environment, has the new zone at the next reading of the clock: in the same clause when no DATE or TIME call came before the change there, and from the next clause otherwise.

numeric digits 20
o = time('O')
say datatype(o, 'W') (abs(o) < 86400000000) (time('O') == time('O', '12:00:00')),
    (time('T') == time('F') % 1000000 - 62135596800) (time('S') == time('T') // 86400)
say time('O', '00:00:00') == time('O', '23:59:59.5', 'L')
say time('O', '7200000000', 'O') time('O', '-7200000000', 'O') time('O', '0', 'O')
signal on syntax name a
say time('O', 'noon')
a: say condition('o')~code

1 1 1 1 1
1
7200000000 -7200000000 0
40.19

numeric digits 20
call value 'TZ', 'UTC', 'ENVIRONMENT'
say time('O')
call value 'TZ', 'UTC-2', 'ENVIRONMENT'
say time('O')
say time('O') value('TZ', 'UTC', 'ENVIRONMENT') time('O')
say time('O')
say value('TZ', 'UTC-2', 'ENVIRONMENT') time('O')

Reading a time

[bif.time.in.text]

The informats N, L and C read the formats that the options of the same letters write, and accept nothing else: no blank or other character before, after or inside the time, and no other number of digits in a field. N has two-digit hours from 00 to 23, minutes from 00 to 59 and seconds from 00 to 59. L has the same, followed by a point and from one to six digits, which are the microseconds when read as if completed on the right with zeros. C has an hour from 1 to 12 written with or without a leading zero, a colon, minutes of two digits from 00 to 59, and am or pm in lower case; 12 with am is midnight, 12 with pm is noon.

say time('N', '23:59:59') time('N', '12:00am', 'C') time('N', '12:30pm', 'C') time('N', '01:30pm', 'C'),
    time('N', '1:30pm', 'C') time('N', '11:59pm', 'C') time('N', '00:30:00')
say time('L', '01:02:03.4', 'L') time('L', '01:02:03.45', 'L') time('L', '01:02:03.000001', 'L')

[bif.time.in.number]

The informats H, M, S, F and T read a count: hours, minutes or seconds since midnight, or the number of microseconds or seconds that F and T write. The string may have any form of a number, such as 5, 5, +5, 5.0 and 5e0, and NUMERIC DIGITS does not apply. A string whose value is a whole number is read as that number, however many leading or trailing zeros it has, and the number must be in the range given below. A string whose value is not a whole number raises SYNTAX 40.19 when it has at most nine significant digits for H, M and S, or at most 18 for F and T, its significant digits being those from the first digit that is not 0 to the last digit that is not 0. This book does not specify whether a string with more significant digits, whose value is not a whole number, is accepted, nor what it then reads as. H must be from 0 to 23, M from 0 to 1439 and S from 0 to 86399. F must be from 0 to 315537897599999999 and T from -62135596800 to 253402300799, which are the instants from 1 January 0001 to 31 December 9999. An F or T names a date and a time, and a format other than F or T keeps only the time of day; F and T keep both.

[bif.time.in.truncate]

A conversion answers the earliest time that fits the string. A part of the time that the string gives and the format of the answer has no place for is dropped, never rounded: N, C, H, M and S drop the microseconds, C, H and M drop the seconds as well, and H drops the minutes. A part that the answer needs and the string lacks is zero.

say time('N', '12:00:59.999999', 'L') time('C', '23:59:59.999999', 'L') time('M', '00:00:59.999999', 'L')
say time('S', '12:00:00.999999', 'L') time('H', '12:59:59', 'N') time('L', '12:34:56')

[bif.time.in.offset]

The informat O reads a whole number of microseconds, as the informats F and T read their counts, as an offset from UTC. The answer is the current time in a zone that far from UTC, as of the moment of the clause: with the offset of the local zone, the current local time. Every offset from -86400000000 to 86400000000, a day either way, is accepted; this book does not specify how much further the range of the offset goes.

numeric digits 20
say (time('F', time('O'), 'O') == time('F')) (time('N', time('O'), 'O') == time('N')),
    (time('F', 3600000000, 'O') - time('F', 0, 'O') == 3600000000),
    (time('T', -7200000000, 'O') - time('T', 0, 'O') == -7200)
say (time('F', 86400000000, 'O') - time('F', 0, 'O') == 86400000000),
    (time('F', -86400000000, 'O') - time('F', 0, 'O') == -86400000000)
